                                                    SECTION-A : ENGLISH LANGUAGE
        Directions (Q.1-Q.24): Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.
        Directions (Q.1-Q.6): The passage below is accompanied by a set of questions. Choose the best answer to
        each question.
        What we would today call cash assistance for the differently abled could in a different era permissibly have been
        called welfare for cripples. The terms welfare and crippled sound somewhere between loaded and abusive today,
        and yet once were considered civil by educated, sensitive people. There actually was an organisation called the
        International Society for the Welfare of Cripples established in 1922.
        However, in 1960 it was retitled the International Society for the Rehabilitation of the Disabled. As appropriate as
        that seems from our vantage point, it demonstrated a general tendency towards which we often roll our eyes. ‘Okay,
        what are we supposed to call it now?’ we sometimes think, as terms considered proper for a group or phenomenon
        seem to change every generation or so. The implication is that we find this rolling terminology a bit much – why
        can’t the names of things just stay put? On disabled, for example, what was wrong with handicapped, and why must
        we now move on to differently abled? Isn’t all of this kind of like Puff Daddy to P Diddy?
        No, actually. What the cognitive psychologist and linguist Steven Pinker has artfully termed ‘the euphemism
        treadmill’ is not a tic or a stunt. It is an inevitable and, more to the point, healthy process, necessary in view of the
        eternal gulf between language and opinion. We think of euphemisms as one-time events, where one prissily coins a
        way of saying something that detracts from something unpleasant about it. That serves perfectly well as a definition
        of what euphemism is, but misses the point that euphemism tends to require regular renewal. This is because
        thought changes more slowly than we can change the words for it, and has a way of catching up with our new
        coinages. Since that is likely eternal, we must accept that we’ll change our terms just like we change our underwear,
        as a part of linguistic life in a civilised society.
        The reason for this rolling semantic renewal is that the meanings of words are, in actual usage, messier than their
        dictionary definitions, cast in the tidy eternity of print, might make them seem. We store words in our brains amid
        webs of association, with experiences, impressions and other words. As a result, a word is always redolent of various
        associations, metaphorical extensions, beyond its core meaning.
        For example, generous once meant noble, with no connection to sharing. It’s what William Shakespeare meant when
        he used the term. So when Edmund in King Lear defends himself against dismissal as low-born by insisting that
        … my dimensions are as well compact,
        My mind as generous, and my shape as true,
        As honest madam’s issue
        it can throw us a bit, making us wonder how a mind can be generous, and we find it a bit curious that someone would
        defend himself against a charge of bastardy by pointing out his magnanimity. However, in earlier societies, the noble
        person was often responsible for a degree of charity to the ordinary population, such that magnanimity was a trait
        associated with nobility. Over time, especially as formal nobility itself had ever less importance (think of the fate of
        the Crawleys in Downton Abbey), the meaning of magnanimity changed from a resonance of generous to the
        meaning it has today.
        A word, then, is like a bell tone, with a central pitch seasoned by overtones. As the tone fades away, the overtones
        can hang in the air. Words are similar, with opinion, assumption and, more to the point, bias as equivalents to the
        overtones. Crippled began as a sympathetic term. However, a sad reality of human society is that there are negative
        associations and even dismissal harboured against those with disabilities. Thus crippled became accreted with those
        overtones, so to speak, to the point that handicapped was fashioned as a replacement term free from such baggage.
        Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from the article, “Euphemise this”.

content.questionText: Which of the following has been asserted by the author?
options:
Linguistic expressions undergo unavoidable cycles of renewal because words continually accumulate social
            connotations that erode their neutrality.

Lexical shifts occur mainly due to arbitrary trends in public taste, resembling superficial changes in popular
            culture.

The meanings of terms can be fixed permanently if dictionaries are treated as the ultimate authority on
            language.

Once introduced, a respectful designation retains its status indefinitely, as the community’s initial intention
            ensures its stability.
content.explanation: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to Linguistic expressions undergo unavoidable cycles of renewal because words continually accumulate social connotations that erode their neutrality. Therefore option A is the answer identified by the official key.

The endurance of a term is determined primarily by the authority of lexicographers who record its fixed
            definition.

Changes in labels for social groups reflect no more than linguistic fads that resemble shifts in celebrity names
            or cultural fashions.

The replacement of older words with newer ones is merely an act of politeness and does not reveal anything
            substantial about thought or society.

The layers of connotation attached to words expose how prejudice and bias seep into language, gradually
            corrupting even initially sympathetic terms.

options:
Establish a standing practice of periodically revising public and institutional terminology in consultation with
            the affected communities, and phase in respectful replacements when existing terms accrue disparaging

        Directions (Q.1-Q.24): Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.
        Directions (Q.1-Q.6): The passage below is accompanied by a set of questions. Choose the best answer to
        each question.
        What we would today call cash assistance for the differently abled could in a different era permissibly have been
        called welfare for cripples. The terms welfare and crippled sound somewhere between loaded and abusive today,
        and yet once were considered civil by educated, sensitive people. There actually was an organisation called the
        International Society for the Welfare of Cripples established in 1922.
        However, in 1960 it was retitled the International Society for the Rehabilitation of the Disabled. As appropriate as
        that seems from our vantage point, it demonstrated a general tendency towards which we often roll our eyes. ‘Okay,
        what are we supposed to call it now?’ we sometimes think, as terms considered proper for a group or phenomenon
        seem to change every generation or so. The implication is that we find this rolling terminology a bit much – why
        can’t the names of things just stay put? On disabled, for example, what was wrong with handicapped, and why must
        we now move on to differently abled? Isn’t all of this kind of like Puff Daddy to P Diddy?
        No, actually. What the cognitive psychologist and linguist Steven Pinker has artfully termed ‘the euphemism
        treadmill’ is not a tic or a stunt. It is an inevitable and, more to the point, healthy process, necessary in view of the
        eternal gulf between language and opinion. We think of euphemisms as one-time events, where one prissily coins a
        way of saying something that detracts from something unpleasant about it. That serves perfectly well as a definition
        of what euphemism is, but misses the point that euphemism tends to require regular renewal. This is because
        thought changes more slowly than we can change the words for it, and has a way of catching up with our new
        coinages. Since that is likely eternal, we must accept that we’ll change our terms just like we change our underwear,
        as a part of linguistic life in a civilised society.
        The reason for this rolling semantic renewal is that the meanings of words are, in actual usage, messier than their
        dictionary definitions, cast in the tidy eternity of print, might make them seem. We store words in our brains amid
        webs of association, with experiences, impressions and other words. As a result, a word is always redolent of various
        associations, metaphorical extensions, beyond its core meaning.
        For example, generous once meant noble, with no connection to sharing. It’s what William Shakespeare meant when
        he used the term. So when Edmund in King Lear defends himself against dismissal as low-born by insisting that
        … my dimensions are as well compact,
        My mind as generous, and my shape as true,
        As honest madam’s issue
        it can throw us a bit, making us wonder how a mind can be generous, and we find it a bit curious that someone would
        defend himself against a charge of bastardy by pointing out his magnanimity. However, in earlier societies, the noble
        person was often responsible for a degree of charity to the ordinary population, such that magnanimity was a trait
        associated with nobility. Over time, especially as formal nobility itself had ever less importance (think of the fate of
        the Crawleys in Downton Abbey), the meaning of magnanimity changed from a resonance of generous to the
        meaning it has today.
        A word, then, is like a bell tone, with a central pitch seasoned by overtones. As the tone fades away, the overtones
        can hang in the air. Words are similar, with opinion, assumption and, more to the point, bias as equivalents to the
        overtones. Crippled began as a sympathetic term. However, a sad reality of human society is that there are negative
        associations and even dismissal harboured against those with disabilities. Thus crippled became accreted with those
        overtones, so to speak, to the point that handicapped was fashioned as a replacement term free from such baggage.

content.passageText:
Passage (Q.7-Q.12): According to the National Institute of Mental Health, nearly a third of U.S. adults have
        experienced at least one form of anxiety disorder at some point in their lives. What is more, anxiety in the United
        States is on the rise with drastic upticks being recorded even in the years leading up to the pandemic. And, yet, while
        psychological measurements and diagnostic manuals can help us to identify and treat those suffering from anxiety,
        they fall well short of explaining it. Indeed, in spite of anxiety’s near-ubiquity Who hasn’t felt anxious at one time or
        another? the concept of anxiety remains opaque.
        Why this is the case may have something to do with the fact that anxiety is incredibly commonplace. We tend not to
        recognize, let alone understand, the things we experience most. More than that, however, is the fact that the cause
        of one’s anxiety is often elusive. Anxiety has a knack for striking when things are going well. In the midst of struggle
        and chaos, it is noticeably absent. But when the calamity subsides and the tension is resolved, only then does it rear
        its menacing head.
        This perplexing attribute garnered the attention of the 19th-century existential philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, who
        devoted multiple works to unpacking anxiety, both theoretically and experientially. For Kierkegaard, anxiety is
        intimately linked with self-reflection our awareness that we exist as individuals and our ability to critically examine
        ourselves. Human beings, he says, possess a capacity that appears to be absent in other living creatures. We are self-
        conscious. Our psyches are not simply directed outward at the world around us. We can pause and reflect upon our
        behavior. We can evaluate ourselves.
        This faculty of self-examination has rightly been lauded throughout the history of human thought. According to
        Plato, “the unexamined life is not worth living,” and part of our job as therapists is to help bring to consciousness
        past experiences that remain repressed and thus hidden from our patients’ conscious lives. Yet, for Kierkegaard, the
        benefits of self-reflection do not come without their drawbacks. To be self-aware, he says, is to be responsible, to
        recognize oneself as being implicated in the lives and, thus, the suffering of others. When we reflect upon ourselves,
        we often notice the ways we have failed to live up to that responsibility, the times we have shirked or even simply
        neglected it.
        Such responsibility, Kierkegaard says, comes from the fact that, as self-conscious beings, we recognize the freedom
        we have to choose between various possibilities. “A tree among trees, a cat among animals,” to use Camus’ famous
        formulation, never reflects upon the fact that it could have acted otherwise. It does not look back and regret its
        choices. What is more, such beings do not anticipate an unrealized future and see the myriad possibilities that lay
        ahead of them.
        Human beings, on the other hand, do. For us, anxiety is about what we have done (or failed to do) and what we might
        do (or fail to do). It is an anxiety about the fact that, as free beings, we live with an infinite number of possibilities
        before us and an infinite number of unrealized possibilities already behind us. While our lives are made up of the
        moments we actually experience, our psyches are racked by possibilities that have never or will never occur.
content.questionText:
How does the passage connect the increase in anxiety disorders in the United States to the existential perspective
        of human freedom and responsibility outlined by Kierkegaard?
options: By suggesting that modern societal pressures diminish our sense of freedom and increase anxiety.
It implies that the rise in anxiety is directly linked to an increase in societal responsibilities.
The passage argues that increased self-awareness in modern times has heightened existential anxiety.
It proposes that the ubiquity of anxiety reflects a deeper, existential crisis about choice and freedom.
content.explanation: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to It proposes that the ubiquity of anxiety reflects a deeper, existential crisis about choice and freedom. Therefore option D is the answer identified by the official key.

content.passageText:
Passage (Q.13-Q.18): Sociology as a science and particularly as a separate field of study is of recent origin. It is the
        youngest of the social sciences. August Comte, the father of sociology, first of conceived the word ‘sociology’ in, 1839.
        He had intended to name the new science social physics, but he rejected this term after a Belgian scholar, Adolphe
        Quetelet, began to make statistical studies of society and to call his area of Endeavour social physics.
        The word sociology is a barbaric combination of Latin word ‘socius’ and Greek word Logus, Logus connotes study
        on a high level and socius points to society. Thus, etymologically, sociology means the study of society on a highly
        generalised or abstract level. In other words, the etymological meaning of sociology is the ‘science of society’.
        Society can be defined as interdependent human beings, making them the subject matter of sociology. While other
        sciences study individuals or groups, they do not explore their interdependence like sociology does.
        Sociology is the science of society as a whole. No other social science endeavours to study society in totality. Social
        sciences like history, economics, political science, anthropology, psychology etc. deal with particular aspect of
        society. Political science deals with political institutions and political activities.
        History deals with unique events relating to past. Economic is concerned with activities relating to production and
        consumption. These social sciences do not give a complete picture of the society. Sociology on the other hand, studies
        society in its entirety.
        It essentially and fundamentally deals with that network of social relationships we call society. Science has been
        defined as a body of knowledge. Sociology is also a body of knowledge about society. Sociology as science of society
        refers to a body of knowledge about society which has been empirically tested. Society may be defined as the
        complicated network and ever-changing pattern of social relationships. Sociology is the science of society, thus
        defined. The scholarly development of sociology has been like walking on thin ice.
        Sociology has been defined in number of ways by different scholars. There are as many definitions of sociology as
        there are sociologists. To understand more fully what sociology is about some of its definitions may be cited as
        follows:
        In 1839, Comte defined sociology as the science of human association or the study of gregarious life. In 1851, he
        attempted to give more flesh and blood to the said definition in his work System of Positive Politics. He conceived


1


        of sociology as an abstract theoretical science of social phenomena. According to him it is the business of sociology
        to discover and abstract social laws and thereby to explain the social phenomena.
        Sociology is the study of groups. According to many sociologists, sociology studies man as a member of the -group
        and as a participant in culture. Man is never an individual in isolation. It has been said that the group is the datum
        of sociology, not the individual human being. Sociology studies human beings in their group relations, human
        behaviour in terms of groups and groupings.
        Sociology, as described by Harry M. Johnson, deals with social groups, their structures, processes of maintenance or
        change, and inter-group relations. It is also defined as the study of social relationships, collective behavior, human
        interactions, and social phenomena. Scholars like Morris Ginsberg and Max Weber view it as the study of human
        interactions and their consequences. However, sociologists have varying perspectives on the essence of sociology,
        as evident from the diverse definitions.

Other social sciences explore society in its entirety, while sociology focuses on specific aspects like politics and

Other social sciences deal with social relationships, while sociology examines the unique events and historical
            aspects of society.

Passage (Q.19-Q.24): The circumstances under which John Stuart Mill wrote his Liberty are largely connected with
        the influence which Mrs. Taylor wielded over his career. The dedication is well known. It contains the most
        extraordinary panegyric on a woman that any philosopher has ever penned. "Were I but capable of interpreting to
        the world one-half the great thoughts and noble feelings which are buried in her grave, I should be the medium of a
        greater benefit to it than is ever likely to arise from anything that I can write, unprompted and unassisted by her all
        but unrivalled wisdom." It is easy for the ordinary worldly cynicism to curl a sceptical lip over sentences like these.
        There may be exaggeration of sentiment, the necessary and inevitable reaction of a man who was trained according
        to the "dry light" of so unimpressionable a man as James Mill, the father; but the passage quoted is not the only one
        in which John Stuart Mill proclaims his unhesitating belief in the intellectual influence of his wife. The treatise on
        Liberty was written especially under her authority and encouragement, but there are many earlier references to the
        power which she exercised over his mind. Mill was introduced to her as early as 1831, at a dinner-party at Mr.
        Taylor's house, where were present, amongst others, Roebuck, W. J. Fox, and Miss Harriet Martineau. The
        acquaintance rapidly ripened into intimacy and the intimacy into friendship, and Mill was never weary of expatiating
        on all the advantages of so singular a relationship. In some of the presentation copies of his work on Political
        Economy, he wrote the following dedication: "To Mrs. John Taylor, who, of all persons known to the author, is the
        most highly qualified either to originate or to appreciate speculation on social advancement, this work is with the
        highest respect and esteem dedicated." An article on the enfranchisement of women was made the occasion for
        another encomium. We shall hardly be wrong in attributing a much later book, The Subjection of Women, published
        in 1869, to the influence wielded by Mrs. Taylor. Finally, the pages of the Autobiography ring with the dithyrambic
        praise of his "almost infallible counsellor."
        The facts of this remarkable intimacy can easily be stated. The deductions are more difficult. There is no question
        that Mill's infatuation was the cause of considerable trouble to his acquaintances and friends. His father openly taxed
        him with being in love with another man's wife. Roebuck, Mrs. Grote, Mrs. Austin, Miss Harriet Martineau were
        amongst those who suffered because they made some allusion to a forbidden subject. Mrs. Taylor lived with her
        daughter in a lodging in the country; but in 1851 her husband died, and then Mill made her his wife. Opinions were
        widely divergent as to her merits; but everyone agreed that up to the time of her death, in 1858, Mill was wholly lost
        to his friends. George Mill, one of Mill's younger brothers, gave it as his opinion that she was a clever and remarkable
        woman, but "nothing like what John took her to be." Carlyle, in his reminiscences, described her with ambiguous
        epithets. She was "vivid," "iridescent," "pale and passionate and sad-looking, a living-romance heroine of the royalist
        volition and questionable destiny."
        Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from the Introduction of Mr. John Stuart Mill’s essay, “On Liberty”, written
        by Mr. W. L. Courtney.

        Passage (Q.25-Q.30): The University Grants Commission (UGC) has taken significant steps to address systemic
        discrimination within higher educational institutions across India. The 2026 regulations represent a comprehensive
        attempt to create an institutional mechanism ensuring dignity, equality, and non-discrimination on campuses. These
        regulations mandate every university and college to establish an Equity Committee tasked with receiving,
        investigating, and resolving complaints related to caste-based harassment and discrimination.
        The regulations draw from constitutional provisions under Articles 14, 15, 17, and 21, reinforcing the principles of
        equality, abolition of untouchability, and protection of life and dignity. Institutions are required to conduct
        mandatory sensitization programs for faculty, staff, and students to foster inclusive campus environments. Failure
        to comply with these regulations may result in withdrawal of recognition or funding by the UGC.
        However, the regulations have sparked considerable debate. Critics argue that the framework lacks adequate
        procedural safeguards, potentially enabling misuse against innocent individuals. Concerns have also been raised
        about the composition and independence of Equity Committees, questioning whether institutional authorities can
        impartially investigate complaints involving their own faculty or administration. Supporters contend that decades
        of documented campus discrimination including social boycotts, verbal abuse, and academic bias necessitate
        strong regulatory intervention. The broader challenge remains balancing victim protection with principles of
        natural justice, ensuring that anti-discrimination mechanisms do not themselves become instruments of injustice.

        Passage (Q.25-Q.30): The University Grants Commission (UGC) has taken significant steps to address systemic
        discrimination within higher educational institutions across India. The 2026 regulations represent a comprehensive
        attempt to create an institutional mechanism ensuring dignity, equality, and non-discrimination on campuses. These
        regulations mandate every university and college to establish an Equity Committee tasked with receiving,
        investigating, and resolving complaints related to caste-based harassment and discrimination.
        The regulations draw from constitutional provisions under Articles 14, 15, 17, and 21, reinforcing the principles of
        equality, abolition of untouchability, and protection of life and dignity. Institutions are required to conduct
        mandatory sensitization programs for faculty, staff, and students to foster inclusive campus environments. Failure
        to comply with these regulations may result in withdrawal of recognition or funding by the UGC.
        However, the regulations have sparked considerable debate. Critics argue that the framework lacks adequate
        procedural safeguards, potentially enabling misuse against innocent individuals. Concerns have also been raised
        about the composition and independence of Equity Committees, questioning whether institutional authorities can
        impartially investigate complaints involving their own faculty or administration. Supporters contend that decades
        of documented campus discrimination including social boycotts, verbal abuse, and academic bias necessitate
        strong regulatory intervention. The broader challenge remains balancing victim protection with principles of
        natural justice, ensuring that anti-discrimination mechanisms do not themselves become instruments of injustice.
content.questionText: Which report first recommended the establishment of a University Grants Committee in India?
options: Kothari Commission Report, 1964
Sargeant Report, 1944
Radhakrishnan Report, 1948
Mudaliar Commission Report, 1952
content.explanation: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to Sargeant Report, 1944. Therefore option B is the answer identified by the official key.

Passage (Q.31-Q.36): The Central Information Commission (CIC), established under the Right to Information Act,
        2005, is the apex appellate body for RTI matters concerning central public authorities. The Commission comprises
        a maximum of 11 members one Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners. For
        years, the CIC operated with significant vacancies, leading to a massive backlog of pending appeals and complaints,
        undermining citizens' fundamental right to information.
        The RTI Amendment Act, 2019 was a landmark change that empowered the Central Government to prescribe the
        tenure, salary, and service conditions of Information Commissioners, replacing the earlier statutory framework.
        Critics argued this diluted the Commission's independence by giving the executive greater control. The full
        constitution of the CIC is expected to reduce pendency, strengthen accountability across government institutions,

1


        and restore public confidence in the transparency framework that the RTI Act envisioned as a cornerstone of
        democratic governance in India.

        leader among emerging economies.

Passage (Q.43-Q.47): A potential American military takeover of Greenland would create unprecedented
        contradictions within the Western alliance. It would directly undermine NATO's Article 5 the principle of collective
        defence which assumes external aggression, not one member violating another's territorial integrity. Denmark,
        which administers Greenland, was among the first to invoke Article 5 after the 9/11 attacks and suffered heavy
        losses fighting alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan, making any such move a profound betrayal.
        Such action would directly benefit Russia by fracturing NATO unity and diverting Western focus from Ukraine
        ironically achieving what Moscow has long sought. Canada would face acute security anxiety, fearing encirclement
        in the Arctic and triggering a classic security dilemma pushing both nations toward militarization.
        The consequences could cascade globally. If NATO fractured, countries like Germany, Poland, South Korea, and Japan
        might reconsider independent nuclear deterrents, pressuring the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Denmark and
        Greenland remain firmly opposed political leaders have declared "Greenland is not for sale" while Greenland's
        indigenous population seeks autonomy, not transfer to another power. Ultimately, such a move would signal that
        might makes right, undermining the rules-based international order the West claims to defend.

Directions (Q.53-Q.82): Read the comprehension carefully and answer the questions.
        Passage (Q.53-Q.57): Aaya Ram Gaya Ram was a phrase that became popular in Indian politics after a Haryana
        MLA Gaya Lal changed his party thrice within the same day in 1967. The anti-defection law sought to prevent such
        political defections which may be due to reward of office or other similar considerations.
        The Tenth Schedule was inserted in the Constitution in 1985. It lays down the process by which legislators may be
        disqualified on grounds of defection by the Presiding Officer of a legislature based on a petition by any other member
        of the House. A legislator is deemed to have defected if he either voluntarily gives up the membership of his party or
        disobeys the directives of the party leadership on a vote. This implies that a legislator defying (abstaining or voting
        against) the party whip on any issue can lose his membership of the House. The law applies to both Parliament and
        state assemblies.
        Legislators may change their party without the risk of disqualification in certain circumstances. The law allows a
        party to merge with or into another party provided that at least two-thirds of its legislators are in favour of the
        merger. In such a scenario, neither the members who decide to merge, nor the ones who stay with the original party
        will face disqualification.
        The anti-defection law seeks to provide a stable government by ensuring the legislators do not switch sides.
        However, this law also restricts a legislator from voting in line with his conscience, judgement and interests of his
        electorate. Such a situation impedes the oversight function of the legislature over the government, by ensuring that
        members vote based on the decisions taken by the party leadership, and not what their constituents would like them
        to vote for.
        Source: https://prsindia.org/theprsblog/the-anti-defection-law-explained?page=34&per-page=1
content.questionText:
Vikram Singh is an MLA belonging to the "Lok Shakti Party" (LSP), which is the ruling party in Rajasthan with 112
        MLAs in the 200-member assembly. During the state budget session in March 2025, the LSP issues a three-line whip
        directing all its members to vote in favor of the budget. Vikram, representing a drought-affected constituency, is
        deeply opposed to certain provisions in the budget that cut allocations for drought relief and irrigation projects.
        Despite his reservations, the party leadership refuses to modify the budget. Vikram decides to vote against the
        budget, following what he believes to be his conscience and the interests of his constituents. The budget passes with
        105 votes in favor. Immediately after the vote, another LSP MLA files a disqualification petition against Vikram with
        the Speaker, citing violation of the party whip. Based on the passage, is Vikram likely to face disqualification under
        the Tenth Schedule?
options:
No, because Vikram voted based on his conscience and the interests of his electorate, which the passage
            recognizes as important considerations for legislators.

Yes, because a legislator is deemed to have defected if he disobeys the directives of the party leadership on a
            vote, and defying the party whip can lead to loss of House membership.

No, because the budget ultimately passed, so Vikram's dissenting vote did not cause the government to fall or
            destabilize governance.

Yes, but only if at least two-thirds of LSP MLAs vote to expel Vikram from the party, following the same threshold
            required for party mergers.

        state assemblies.

Passage (Q.58-Q.62): Civil courts in India generally allow any person to sue to enforce a civil right, but the Code of
        Civil Procedure creates special rules when the litigant is an alien or when the dispute involves foreign States, foreign
        rulers, ambassadors, or envoys. The basic idea is to balance access to justice with concerns of sovereignty,
        diplomatic relations, and national security.
        Under Section 83 CPC, an “alien friend” (a foreign national from a country not at war with India) may sue in an Indian
        court as if they were an Indian citizen. By contrast, an “alien enemy” faces restrictions: if such a person is residing
        in India, they may sue only with the permission of the Central Government, and if they are residing in a foreign
        country, they generally cannot sue in Indian courts.
        The Code also recognises that foreign States may sometimes need to approach Indian courts. Section 84 permits a
        foreign State to sue in a competent court, especially where the suit is meant to enforce a private right vested in its
        ruler or an officer acting in a public capacity. Since a foreign ruler cannot personally appear and conduct litigation
        in India, Section 85 allows the Central Government to appoint persons to prosecute or defend suits on behalf of such
        rulers, ensuring the court knows who can validly represent them.
        However, when the suit is against a foreign ruler, ambassador, or envoy, the law is stricter. Section 86 provides that
        such a suit cannot ordinarily be instituted in a competent court without the consent of the Central Government,
        certified in writing, reflecting a limited form of sovereign/diplomatic immunity.
        These rules matter because they determine not only who may sue, but also when the judiciary must defer to
        executive certification in matters touching foreign relations.
        (Source- https://lawbhoomi.com/suits-by-aliens-and-by-or-against-foreign-rulers-ambassadors-and-envoys/)

Passage (Q.63-Q.67): Indian consumer law treats a buyer of goods or user of services as more than a market
        participant, it treats them as a rights-holder. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 recognises six core consumer
        rights: the right to safety, right to be informed, right to choose, right to be heard, right to seek redressal, and right
        to consumer education/awareness. These rights aim to correct the information and power imbalance between
        sellers and consumers, especially in markets where advertising, packaging, and online interfaces can influence
        decisions more than actual product quality.
        Each right has a practical role. Right to Safety means the consumer’s right to be protected against the marketing of
        goods and services that are hazardous to life and property. Products and services should meet not only a consumer’s
        immediate needs but also their long-term interests. Before purchasing, consumers should insist on quality and
        warranties/guarantees, and preferably buy quality-certified items such as ISI or AGMARK marked products.
        Right to be Informed, Right to Choose, and Right to be Heard together ensure fairness in the marketplace. The Right
        to be informed means the consumer must be told the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of
        goods/services so they are protected against unfair trade practices; consumers should seek complete information
        before deciding to avoid high-pressure selling. The Right to Choose means access (wherever possible) to a variety
        of goods and services at competitive prices, and in monopoly situations, assurance of satisfactory quality and fair
        pricing, including access to basic goods and services. The Right to be Heard ensures that consumer interests receive
        due consideration at appropriate forums and includes representation in bodies formed for consumer welfare, which
        can be strengthened through non-political, non-commercial consumer organisations.
        Right to Seek Redressal means the right to fair settlement of genuine grievances and remedies against unfair trade
        practices or exploitation; even small individual complaints can have a large social impact, and consumers may take
        help from consumer organisations. Right to Consumer Education means the right to acquire knowledge and skills
        to remain an informed consumer throughout life; ignorance—especially in rural areas—often leads to exploitation,
        so awareness and exercise of rights is essential for effective consumer protection.
        Source- https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/consumer-rights?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Nisha purchases a new pressure cooker from "KitchenMart," a popular online marketplace. The product does not
        carry any ISI certification mark. After using it twice, the cooker's safety valve malfunctions during cooking, causing
        steam burns to Nisha's hands. She later discovers that the manufacturer had received multiple complaints about the
        same defect but continued selling the product without any warning label or recall. Nisha approaches a consumer
        forum claiming that her Right to Safety has been violated. KitchenMart argues that since Nisha purchased the
        product voluntarily without checking for certification marks, she assumed the risk and cannot claim any consumer
        rights. Based on the passage, is Nisha's claim regarding violation of Right to Safety likely to succeed?
options:
Yes, because the Right to Safety means the consumer's right to be protected against marketing of goods that are
            hazardous to life and property, and the defective pressure cooker caused burns to Nisha.

No, because Nisha failed to insist on quality-certified items such as ISI marked products before purchasing, as
            the passage advises consumers should do.

Yes, because KitchenMart is an online marketplace, and the passage specifically states that online interfaces
            influence decisions more than actual product quality.

No, because the Right to Safety only applies to services that are hazardous, not to goods like pressure cookers
            which are physical products.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the Right to Safety means the consumer's right to be protected against marketing of goods that are hazardous to life and property, and the defective pressure cooker caused burns to Nisha. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

        participant, it treats them as a rights-holder. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 recognises six core consumer
        rights: the right to safety, right to be informed, right to choose, right to be heard, right to seek redressal, and right
        to consumer education/awareness. These rights aim to correct the information and power imbalance between
        sellers and consumers, especially in markets where advertising, packaging, and online interfaces can influence
        decisions more than actual product quality.
        Each right has a practical role. Right to Safety means the consumer’s right to be protected against the marketing of
        goods and services that are hazardous to life and property. Products and services should meet not only a consumer’s
        immediate needs but also their long-term interests. Before purchasing, consumers should insist on quality and
        warranties/guarantees, and preferably buy quality-certified items such as ISI or AGMARK marked products.
        Right to be Informed, Right to Choose, and Right to be Heard together ensure fairness in the marketplace. The Right
        to be informed means the consumer must be told the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of
        goods/services so they are protected against unfair trade practices; consumers should seek complete information
        before deciding to avoid high-pressure selling. The Right to Choose means access (wherever possible) to a variety
        of goods and services at competitive prices, and in monopoly situations, assurance of satisfactory quality and fair
        pricing, including access to basic goods and services. The Right to be Heard ensures that consumer interests receive
        due consideration at appropriate forums and includes representation in bodies formed for consumer welfare, which
        can be strengthened through non-political, non-commercial consumer organisations.
        Right to Seek Redressal means the right to fair settlement of genuine grievances and remedies against unfair trade
        practices or exploitation; even small individual complaints can have a large social impact, and consumers may take
        help from consumer organisations. Right to Consumer Education means the right to acquire knowledge and skills
        to remain an informed consumer throughout life; ignorance—especially in rural areas—often leads to exploitation,
        so awareness and exercise of rights is essential for effective consumer protection.
        Source- https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/consumer-rights?utm_source=chatgpt.com
content.questionText:
A consumer advocacy group called "JanAdhikar" files a public interest complaint before the National Consumer
        Disputes Redressal Commission regarding misleading advertisements by a major telecom company. The telecom
        company objects, arguing that JanAdhikar is a registered NGO with political affiliations to an opposition party and
        therefore lacks standing to represent consumer interests. JanAdhikar counters that any organization working for
        consumer welfare can represent consumer interests. Based on the passage, does the telecom company's objection
        regarding JanAdhikar's political affiliation have merit?
options:
No, because the Right to be Heard allows any organization to represent consumers at appropriate forums,
            regardless of their political or commercial affiliations.

Yes, because the passage states that consumer representation should be strengthened through non-political,
            non-commercial consumer organisations.

No, because the Right to Seek Redressal allows consumers to take help from any consumer organisation without
            restrictions.

Yes, because the passage specifically prohibits political parties from filing complaints on behalf of consumers
            under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Yes, because the passage states that consumer representation should be strengthened through non-political, non-commercial consumer organisations. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

Dharampal, an elderly farmer in a village in Uttar Pradesh, purchases pesticide from a local dealer who assures him
        that the product is "government approved" and "100% effective." The dealer does not provide any written
        information about proper usage, safety precautions, or potential crop damage from overuse. Dharampal, unable to
        read English and unaware of his rights, uses the pesticide in excessive quantities, resulting in destruction of his
        entire cotton crop. When he complains, the dealer says that Dharampal should have asked for instructions and that
        illiterate farmers cannot expect detailed explanations. Based on the passage, which observation about consumer
        protection in rural areas is relevant to Dharampal's situation?
options:
Rural consumers like Dharampal have fewer consumer rights than urban consumers because the Consumer
              Protection Act, 2019 primarily applies to educated buyers.

The dealer is correct that consumers have a duty to ask for instructions, and sellers have no obligation to provide
              information unless specifically requested.

Dharampal cannot claim any consumer rights because he purchased agricultural inputs, which are not covered
              under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

The passage recognizes that ignorance especially in rural areas often leads to exploitation, so awareness and
              exercise of rights is essential for effective consumer protection.


1

content.passageText:
Passage (Q.68-Q.72): The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines a partnership as a relationship between two or
        more individuals who comply with share the profits of a business run by them all or by one or more individuals
        acting for all. Individuals who have entered into a partnership with each other are called “partners” and collectively
        a “company,” and also the name under which their business is carried on is termed as the “company name.”
        The relation of partnership arises from contract and not from status; and, in particular, the members of a Hindu
        undivided family carrying on a family business as such, or a Burmese Buddhist husband and wife carrying on
        business as such are not partners in such business.
        If there is no clause to establish a partnership at the expiry of a partnership, it is referred to as a partnership at will.
        Under Section 7 of The Indian Partnership Act, 1932, two conditions have to be met for a partnership to be a
        partnership at will and they are:
        •    There is no agreement on a fixed period for the existence of a partnership.
        •    No provision is made for establishing a partnership.
        If a partnership has been established and continues to operate beyond the fixed period, the partnership will become
        a partnership at will after the end of that term.
        A partnership may be formed for ongoing business or a specific purpose. If the partnership is merely formed to hold
        out one company or complete one undertaking, it’s referred to as a specific partnership. The partnership is going to
        be dissolved after the completion of the said venture or activity. The partners may, however, conform to continue
        the said partnership. But within the absence of this, when the task is complete, the partnership ends.
content.questionText:
Mira and Zain run a small thrift page on Instagram. They agree to split profits from sales, and Zain handles sourcing
        while Mira manages packaging and customer DMs “for both of them.” They never register anything, but both treat
        it as a joint business. Based on the passage, the best description is:
options: A partnership exists because they agreed to share profits from a business run by them or any of them for all.
No partnership exists because a partnership can arise only through registration and public notice.
No partnership exists because only a “company” can share profits and partnerships are not recognised.
A partnership exists only if the business is carried on by all partners personally at all times.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: A partnership exists because they agreed to share profits from a business run by them or any of them for all. Accordingly, option A is the keyed legal result.

The Bansal family runs a popular family restaurant in Indore under the name “Bansal Da Dhaba.” It is managed as a
        Family business. The eldest member decides the menu and finances, while younger members handle billing and
        delivery tie-ups.
        For the last two years, the family has been splitting the restaurant’s earnings in fixed proportions. They also created
        an internal Google Sheet titled “Partner Profit Split” and sometimes introduce family members to suppliers as
        “partners,” to negotiate better credit. However, there is no separate partnership deed or contract among them
        stating that they are partners, and they continue to describe the restaurant as a “family business.” According to the
        passage, which statement is the most accurate?
options:
They are partners because they call each other partners and maintain a “partner profit split” record to share
            earnings.

They are not partners as such, because partnership arises from contract, not status, and HUF members running
            a family business are excluded.

They are partners because they share profits in fixed proportions and one member manages the business on
            behalf of all.

They are not partners because a partnership can exist only if the business is registered under a “company name”
            with authorities.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: They are not partners as such, because partnership arises from contract, not status, and HUF members running a family business are excluded. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

Four creators — Ayaan, Tara, Neha, and Kabir — sign a written agreement to run a paid online course business for
        one year. The agreement fixes the term as one year, but does not mention what happens after that. After the year
        ends, the creators continue selling the same course, collecting subscription revenue, and splitting profits in the same
        ratio. They do not sign any renewal document, and they still have no clause explaining how the partnership will end.
        According to the passage, after the fixed term ends, the partnership is best treated as:
options: A partnership at will after the end of the term, since it continued beyond the fixed period without fresh terms.

Automatically dissolved at the end of the term, because the partnership was formed for a fixed period and
            renewal needs a new contract.

A specific partnership, because the partners are continuing only the same single course venture they originally
            set out to complete.

A partnership at will only if the partners explicitly agree in writing that the fixed-term partnership will convert
            into an at-will partnership.

content.passageText:
Passage (Q.73-Q.77): An “agent” is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealing
        with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the “principal”. The
        contract between Principal and Agent is called ‘Contract of Agency’. Subsequent to the contract, the rights and duties
        of the principal and agent emerge. Authority of an agent can be both express and implied. According to Section 187,
        the authority is said to be express when it is given by words spoken or written. According to Section 187, authority
        is said to be implied when it is to be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case. In carrying out the work
        of the Principal, the agent can take any legal action. That is, the agent can do any lawful thing necessary to carry out
        the work of the Principal.
        An agency relationship is built on mutual trust: the agent acts on behalf of the principal, and in return the principal
        must treat the agent fairly. The rights and duties of an agent and principal therefore move together. Indian contract
        law recognises that when an agent performs the work of the agency, the agent is generally entitled to be paid. Under
        Section 219, an agent is entitled to receive remuneration. However, Section 220 makes an important limitation: if
        the agent is guilty of misconduct in the business of the agency, the agent is not entitled to any remuneration for that
        part of the business in which the misconduct occurred. Thus, remuneration depends not only on performance, but
        also on proper conduct.
        To secure payment and reimbursement, an agent is also given protective rights. Under Section 221, in the absence
        of a contract to the contrary, an agent has a right of lien. This means the agent may retain the goods, papers, and
        other property of the principal that the agent has received, until the agent’s dues—such as commission,
        disbursements, or charges for services relating to that property—are paid or properly accounted for. The lien is
        therefore a practical safeguard, preventing a principal from taking back the property while leaving the agent unpaid.
        The principal’s responsibility is not limited to payment. Under Section 222, the principal must indemnify the agent
        against the consequences of lawful acts done by the agent in exercise of authority. Indemnity here means that the
        principal must make good the loss suffered by the agent when the agent acts lawfully within the authority given.
        Further, Section 225 protects the agent where harm is caused due to the principal’s fault: the principal must
        compensate the agent for injuries suffered because of the principal’s neglect or want of skill. In short, agency law
        ensures that an agent who acts properly is paid, protected, and reimbursed, while an agent who commits misconduct
        cannot demand reward for the tainted part of the agency work.

1
content.questionText:
Vikram is a real estate agent engaged by Priya, a property owner, to sell her three apartments in Mumbai. The agreed
        commission is 2% of the sale value for each apartment sold. Vikram successfully sells the first apartment for ₹1.5
        crore after conducting proper due diligence and transparent negotiations. For the second apartment, Vikram
        secretly accepts a ₹2 lakh bribe from the buyer to undervalue the property, causing Priya to sell it at ₹80 lakh instead
        of its market value of ₹1.2 crore. For the third apartment, Vikram again conducts himself properly and sells it for
        ₹1.8 crore at fair market value. When Vikram claims his 2% commission on all three apartments, Priya refuses to
        pay any commission, arguing that his misconduct in the second transaction taints the entire agency relationship.
        Based on the passage, is Priya's refusal to pay any commission legally justified?
options:
Yes, because once an agent commits misconduct in any part of the agency business, the agent forfeits all
             remuneration for the entire agency relationship, not just the tainted transaction.

No, because under Section 220, an agent is not entitled to remuneration only for that part of the business in
             which the misconduct occurred, meaning Vikram can still claim commission for the first and third apartments.

Yes, because the passage states that agency is built on mutual trust, and Vikram's breach of trust in the second
             transaction destroys the entire foundation of the agency contract.

No, because Section 219 provides an absolute right to remuneration for any agent who performs work, and
             misconduct only affects the agent's liability for damages, not the right to be paid.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: No, because under Section 220, an agent is not entitled to remuneration only for that part of the business in which the misconduct occurred, meaning Vikram can still claim commission for the first and third…. Accordingly, option B is the keyed legal result.

        with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the “principal”. The
        contract between Principal and Agent is called ‘Contract of Agency’. Subsequent to the contract, the rights and duties
        of the principal and agent emerge. Authority of an agent can be both express and implied. According to Section 187,
        the authority is said to be express when it is given by words spoken or written. According to Section 187, authority
        is said to be implied when it is to be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case. In carrying out the work
        of the Principal, the agent can take any legal action. That is, the agent can do any lawful thing necessary to carry out
        the work of the Principal.

        must treat the agent fairly. The rights and duties of an agent and principal therefore move together. Indian contract
        law recognises that when an agent performs the work of the agency, the agent is generally entitled to be paid. Under
        Section 219, an agent is entitled to receive remuneration. However, Section 220 makes an important limitation: if
        the agent is guilty of misconduct in the business of the agency, the agent is not entitled to any remuneration for that
        part of the business in which the misconduct occurred. Thus, remuneration depends not only on performance, but
        also on proper conduct.

        of a contract to the contrary, an agent has a right of lien. This means the agent may retain the goods, papers, and
        other property of the principal that the agent has received, until the agent’s dues—such as commission,
        disbursements, or charges for services relating to that property—are paid or properly accounted for. The lien is
        therefore a practical safeguard, preventing a principal from taking back the property while leaving the agent unpaid.

        ensures that an agent who acts properly is paid, protected, and reimbursed, while an agent who commits misconduct
        cannot demand reward for the tainted part of the agency work.

Passage (Q.78 – Q.82): In our country, a certain section of people has been particularly denounced to such an extent
        that their social advancement has historically lagged behind. Hence the communities which had the privilege of
        being considered genuine at that time, certainly have made a lot of progress both in the social as well as an
        educational arena. Dr. B.R Ambedkar in his speech clearly acknowledged the fact that there is an absence of socio-
        economic equality which is rooted in the system of our society. Hence, the Constitution provided reservation of seats
        in the educational institutions and in public employment to three categories of people - Persons who are socially
        and educationally backward classes (SEBCs) of citizens, scheduled castes and scheduled tribes. It was the S.R. Sinha
        Commission which in 2010 submitted a report on the need for a constitutional amendment for the purpose of giving
        reservation to the general category poor in education as well as in government jobs. For the purpose of upliftment
        of the economically weaker section (EWS) of the society, the Government has instituted a 10 per cent reservation
        by mean of the One hundred and third Constitutional Amendment Act that introduce economic based reservation.
        The main implication of the EWS reservation is that Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution now stand amended,
        empowering the state to provide a maximum of 10 per cent reservation for the economically weaker sections of the
        society excluding the SCs, STs and the OBS-NCL (non-creamy layer). To avail this EWS reservation, an individual
        needs to have a gross family income that is less than Rs. 8 lakh, if they have agricultural land it needs to be below 5
        acres, and a residential plot below 1000 square foot. The reservation policy in the process of bringing different
        sections of society to the same level, should not take away people’s right to equality in the first place. Our
        constitution makers were conscious of this fact and hence they brought a certain limit to the policy of caste
        reservation, i.e., a ceiling of fifty percent. This was first clearly defined in the case of M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
        wherein the court realised that the constitution-makers did assume the fact the caste reservation policy would not
        be misused to provide unreasonable, excessive or extravagant reservation. Breaching the ceiling would hence result
        in a reverse discrimination process and therefore unconstitutional.

        reservation or not?

Their sons will not get the benefits of EWS reservation as the family income of the sons is more than the
            eligibility criteria to claim the said reservation.

Their sons will not get the benefits of EWS reservation as they don’t belong to the poor general category of
            society.

Their sons will get the benefits of EWS reservation as all the essentials have been fulfilled for availing the
            benefits of EWS as per the Act.

Sufficient information regarding the family income of A and B has not been given in the facts therefore decision
            can’t be taken on EWS reservation.

Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

SECTION I
L	To be part of Zimbabwe’s “Born Free” generation was to be handed a promise: that your life
would no longer be shaped by colonial rule. Skin colour would not dictate the right to vote,
learn or work. For Simukai Chigudu, born in 1986, six years after independence, that promise
was stamped on him from the very beginning: “Your name, Simukai, it means to stand up,” his
father, a former liberation fighter, tells him.
Yet, as Chigudu reflects in his compelling memoir, the end of colonial rule does not mean
freedom from historical events and how they reverberate in everyday life. He tells two
interlinked stories: Zimbabwe’s brutal war of independence, and his own search for belonging
in the years that followed. It is a wide-ranging, restless book, passing through Uganda,
Rwanda, Ireland and Mexico City. Yet at its centre are Zimbabwe and Britain, “former colony
and metropole”, and the unfinished business between them.
Chigudu’s parents, who became part of the growing post-independence black middle class,
enrol him in elite private schools. There, he acquires what he calls a “delicate, papery accent”,
plays “white people’s sports” and learns the codes of respectability that promise safety but not
belonging. He comes to appreciate early on that to be black is to be defined by others. Black
Zimbabweans dismiss him as a “salad” for his adopted white habits (such as eating salad).
White Zimbabweans call him a soutpiel, or “salt penis”; for having one foot in Africa, one in
Europe, his genitals “[dangling] in the Mediterranean Sea”. In Britain, a student labels him
“the whitest black man” they know. The burden of his generation’s inheritance is expressed
most powerfully in descriptions of his grandfather’s murder — “they shot him in cold blood and
jettisoned his remains in a shallow pit” — and his father Tafi’s torture under the racist
Rhodesian government. Tafi joined the armed struggle and spent years in exile. “I felt the
weight of history, my life as the gift of his having survived colossal violence,” Chigudu writes.

content.passageText:
Il.	Open up any social media app on your phone and it won’t be long before you scroll to a short
video clip that shows animals and humans sharing a bizarre encounter. While an AI-generated
video of a man taking an underwater selfie with a shark is easy to identify as fake, more
realistic Gen AI videos can warp the way we think about wild animals and their behavioural
traits, putting both us and them in danger. This is thanks to a barrage of Generative AI tools
that allow users to enter text prompts in everyday language and churn out hyper-realistic
videos at scale that can be easily uploaded online. As platforms like Meta pivot to short-form
videos in an attempt to surpass TikTok, while X rewards virality and engagement, users are
incentivised to make and share more low-cost, low-effort content.
As a result, you might have seen gorillas breaking out of zoo enclosures, crocodiles gobbling up
their handlers, dying lions surrendering their cubs to humans, fishermen rescuing polar bears,
and monkeys dancing with children. These videos are generally called “AI slop” due to their

low-grade entertainment value and short length. Often shared with sensationalised captions
or presented as though they are real news events, viewers inevitably waste their time trying to
figure out if the content is real or AI generated. Violence is also a major pull factor in AI
animal videos: a giraffe is decapitated by an overhead bridge, a gorilla smashes a tiger with a
boulder, a hippo excretes in the face of another animal with the power of a missile, a crazed
shark mauls a swimmer, and a whale swims after a desperate Arctic fox. Such videos come
with or without melodramatic storylines. These are reshared, repeated, and re-adapted by
others hoping to go viral. Al-generated animal videos rack up millions of views on platforms
like X and YouTube, because they are seen by viewers across age groups and with varying
levels of media education and digital literacy. In essence, AI animal videos can change our
relationships with animals. [Word Count: 342]

tech/technology /the-dangers-of-ai-animal-slop-videos-explained /article70714858.ece

Il.	Open up any social media app on your phone and it won’t be long before you scroll to a short
video clip that shows animals and humans sharing a bizarre encounter. While an AI-generated
video of a man taking an underwater selfie with a shark is easy to identify as fake, more
realistic Gen AI videos can warp the way we think about wild animals and their behavioural
traits, putting both us and them in danger. This is thanks to a barrage of Generative AI tools
that allow users to enter text prompts in everyday language and churn out hyper-realistic
videos at scale that can be easily uploaded online. As platforms like Meta pivot to short-form
videos in an attempt to surpass TikTok, while X rewards virality and engagement, users are
incentivised to make and share more low-cost, low-effort content.
As a result, you might have seen gorillas breaking out of zoo enclosures, crocodiles gobbling up
their handlers, dying lions surrendering their cubs to humans, fishermen rescuing polar bears,
and monkeys dancing with children. These videos are generally called “AI slop” due to their

low-grade entertainment value and short length. Often shared with sensationalised captions
or presented as though they are real news events, viewers inevitably waste their time trying to
figure out if the content is real or AI generated. Violence is also a major pull factor in AI
animal videos: a giraffe is decapitated by an overhead bridge, a gorilla smashes a tiger with a
boulder, a hippo excretes in the face of another animal with the power of a missile, a crazed
shark mauls a swimmer, and a whale swims after a desperate Arctic fox. Such videos come
with or without melodramatic storylines. These are reshared, repeated, and re-adapted by
others hoping to go viral. Al-generated animal videos rack up millions of views on platforms
like X and YouTube, because they are seen by viewers across age groups and with varying
levels of media education and digital literacy. In essence, AI animal videos can change our
relationships with animals. [Word Count: 342]

tech/technology /the-dangers-of-ai-animal-slop-videos-explained /article70714858.ece

to subtly distort how something is understood

content.passageText:
Il.	In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been
turning over in my mind ever since.
‘Whenever you feel like criticizing any one,’ he told me, ‘just remember that all the people in
this world haven’t had the advantages that you've had.’
He didn’t say any more but we’ve always been unusually communicative in a reserved way,
and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence I’m inclined to
reserve all judgments, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made
me the victim of not a few veteran bores. The abnormal mind is quick to detect and attach
itself to this quality when it appears in a normal person, and so it came about that in college I
was unjustly accused of being a politician, because I was privy to the secret griefs of wild,
unknown men. Most of the confidences were unsought—frequently I have feigned sleep,
preoccupation, or a hostile levity when I realized by some unmistakable sign that an intimate
revelation was quivering on the horizon—for the intimate revelations of young men or at least
the terms in which they express them are usually plagiaristic and marred by obvious
suppressions. Reserving judgments is a matter of infinite hope. I am still a little afraid of
missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat
a sense of the fundamental decencies is parcelled out unequally at birth.
And, after boasting this way of my tolerance, I come to the admission that it has a limit.
Conduct may be founded on the hard rock or the wet marshes but after a certain point I don’t
care what it’s founded on. When I came back from the East last autumn I felt that I wanted
the world to be in uniform and at a sort of moral attention forever; I wanted no more riotous
excursions with privileged glimpses into the human heart. Only Gatsby, the man who gives
his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction—Gatsby who represented everything for
which I have an unaffected scorn. [Word Count: 364]
Source: Extracted with: The Great Gatsby By F. Scott Fitzgerald

options: Background fully excuses all later conduct.
Circumstance explains conduct, but not justifiably.
Confession usually reveals genuine inner truth.
Tolerance mainly protects one from boredom.
content.explanation: This option captures the narrator’s balanced position most accurately. He accepts that conduct may arise from different backgrounds and conditions, yet he refuses to let such causes justify everything.

IV.	The importance of protecting nature is not up for debate. One in six species in Britain is
threatened with extinction. Since 1970, more than half our flowering plants have decreased in
areas where they once thrived. In the 1950s, Britain’s hedgehog population was 30m strong.
Now, it is believed to be under a million. All this demands action. The problem is that a lot of
the action we’ve taken — mainly in the form of legislation — fails to target the biggest drivers of
nature loss. Instead, it bites when we try to build: wind turbines, solar farms, railways or
nuclear power plants, making their construction lengthier, more expensive or, in some cases,
impossible.
You'll notice that these are all examples of green infrastructure — precisely the things we'll
need more of in order to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, which ultimately cause habitat loss on
a massive scale. Greening the grid and providing clean electricity to homes, transport and
industry is one of the most urgent tasks facing us. The only way to do it without generating a
cost-of-living crisis that would dwarf our current predicament (and cause an anti-green
backlash) is to get building — and fast. At the moment, that’s proving far too difficult — and the
obstacles include those well-intentioned laws designed to guard habitats against unchecked
development. Not only do they block the green building we desperately need — they don’t even
do a good job of protecting nature. The money spent on them could transform conservation if
used differently, but instead, it’s effectively thrown away. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Why do our environmental laws end up creating these bizarre situations? The problem is their
inflexibility. They are designed to prevent specific harms caused by specific developments.
This approach only makes sense if building is one of the main drivers of nature loss. But it
isn’t, for a simple reason: we don’t, and almost certainly never will, do enough of it. Less than
6% of Britain is built on. If Labour succeeds in building 1.5m homes, the total amount of built-
up land would only increase by a few hundredths of a percent. Even if you tripled the rate, it
would take decades before even a tenth of Britain was built on. Far more of it, nearly two
thirds, is dedicated to agriculture. [Word Count: 377]

VI.	The country’s 7th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity shows progress in
forest cover and ecosystem restoration, assessing progress towards global biodiversity goals set
for 2030. India reports gains in forest cover, ecosystem restoration and some species recovery,
including tigers and rhinos. However, land degradation, data gaps and limited conservation
coverage remain major challenges for meeting biodiversity commitments.
The report is the country’s official submission under the CBD, an international environmental
treaty through which nations commit to conserving biological diversity and using natural
resources sustainably. All parties to the convention are required to submit periodic reports
outlining what actions they have taken, what progress they have achieved and what
challenges remain.

India is one of the world’s megadiverse countries, with ecosystems ranging from the
Himalayan mountains to coastal mangroves and tropical forests, underlining the importance
of the report. Its biodiversity performance has a substantial influence on global outcomes.
Data from the report will feed into international assessments examining whether the world is
on track to meet biodiversity commitments and identifying any gaps in monitoring systems
and governance that could affect long-term conservation efforts. However, the report also
highlights significant challenges. Monitoring biodiversity is complex and expensive, and
several new indicators still lack standardised protocols. Different ministries collect data at
varying intervals, while rapid improvements in satellite technology can make comparisons
across years difficult. These factors can affect the consistency of datasets and the long-term
comparability of trends. The report provided a broad picture of policy alignment, measurable
progress, data trends and gaps in India’s biodiversity strategy. [Word Count: 258]

in just 18 balls, making it the fastest of this edition and the fastest in a T20 World Cup
knockout game. Sanju Samson hit 24 sixes through the tournament, the most in a single T20
World Cup edition. Sahibzada Farhan and Fakhar Zaman put on a 176-run opening stand
during Pakistan’s Super Eight clash against Sri Lanka. It stands as the highest partnership
for any wicket in T20Is. [Word Count: 247]

VIII. Amid the prevailing situation in West Asia, the Government has invoked the Essential
Commodities Act 1955 to regulate the production, maintain supply, equitable distribution and
availability of natural gas for priority sectors. As per a notification of the Petroleum and
Natural Gas Ministry, the priority of supply of natural gas has been given to sectors and other
essential pipeline operational requirements. It stated that the supply shall be maintained
subject to operational availability to 100 per cent of their past six month average gas
consumption.
The order further states that the government shall ensure the supply of natural gas to the
fertiliser plants on 70 per cent of their past six-month average gas consumption, subject to
operational availability. It added that gas marketing entities shall ensure that gas supply to
tea industries, manufacturing and other industrial consumers supplied through the national
gas grid is maintained at 80 per cent of their past six-month average gas consumption, subject
to operational availability.
The order also stated that all City Gas Distribution entities shall ensure that industrial and
commercial consumers supplied through their networks receive 80 per cent of their past six-
month average gas consumption, subject to operational availability. The ministry also stated
that it has constituted a committee of three executive directors from oil marketing companies
to review the representations for LPG supply to restaurants/hotels/other industries. If the
supply of essential commodities or products were disrupted due to hoarding or black
marketing, this would affect the normal, everyday life of people. [Word Count: 249]

content.questionText:
Which of the following statements correctly reflects the constitutional change introduced by
the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 regarding the office of Governor?
options:
The amendment introduced a system requiring each State to elect its Governor through a
special constitutional process.

The amendment established that Governors must be appointed separately for each State
without any overlapping responsibilities.

The amendment enabled the appointment of the same person as Governor for two or more
States at the same time.

The amendment required Governors to hold independent executive authority over
neighbouring Union Territories.
content.explanation: The Constitution originally stated that there shall be a Governor for each State under Article 153 of the Constitution of India. However, the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956 clarified that nothing in this provision prevents the appointment of the same individual as Governor for two or more States simultaneously.

Commission lacks power because only Parliament may fill gaps, so any direction without

Direction is invalid because electoral instructions must follow statutory rules, and silence

The court should decline because it bars judicial interference during the election process
except by election petitions after completion of elections.

The court may intervene because nomination rejection violates natural justice, and
constitutional rights allow immediate writ relief despite ongoing elections today.

Court must stay the poll because any illegality voids the election, and prevention is better
than later petitions always anyway.

matters, which lie exclusively with Supreme Court alone always.
