content.questionText:
In a coastal district, the Electoral Registration Officer deletes names of several women from
the electoral roll after receiving a complaint that they married into another caste community
and “should vote elsewhere.” The women still reside in the same constituency and have valid
documents. The officer says deletion is needed to preserve “community purity” and prevent
local tension. The women seek restoration, claiming the deletions are discriminatory.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Officer may exclude because local custom controls rolls, and caste based screening
preserves community harmony during elections in villages lawfully.

Exclusion is unlawful because only Election Commission can decide roll entries, and
officers have no power to revise them ever.

Officer must exclude because voter rolls are privileges, and state may choose eligible
groups to avoid fraudulent entries at will.

Exclusion is unlawful because it prohibits exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of
religion, race, caste, or sex for citizens.

Since the deletion is based on caste-linked marriage and targets women, it falls within the prohibited grounds.

Commission must intervene because municipal elections affect democracy, and Article 324
powers extend to every electoral body nationwide without exception.

Commission does not conduct elections to Panchayats and Municipalities, because separate

Commission must act because it administers all elections, and any local poll is part of

party’s symbol for repeated Model Code violations. Two Election Commissioners vote to
suspend; the Chief Election Commissioner dissents and issues a press note stating his view
will “override” the majority because he heads the body. The party relies on the press note and
challenges the suspension as invalid, claiming the majority decision cannot stand.
Which statement is most accurate?

Decision stands because decisions are taken by majority, and the Chief Election
Commissioner has no overriding power over the others.

Decision fails because Chief Election Commissioner is chair, so his dissent nullifies any
majority view automatically every time in law.

Decision stands only if unanimous, because electoral fairness requires consensus, and split
votes show bias and invalidity always for citizens.

Decision fails because dissent triggers judicial review immediately, and courts may
substitute their preference for the minority opinion right away.

In 2025, the President appoints a new Election Commissioner after receiving
recommendations from the Prime Minister and a Union Minister nominated by him. The
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha is not consulted despite being in office. A public-
interest petitioner challenges the appointment process as incomplete and claims the
appointment is void. The Union argues the President’s appointment power is independent and
committee procedure is only directory.
Which statement is most accurate?
options:
Appointment is valid because President appoints independently, and any committee is
advisory only; omission of one member cannot matter legally here today.

Appointment is valid because PM’s minister can replace Opposition Leader, and selection
committee may be two-member for convenience always in practice too.

Appointment is invalid because it needs recommendation of selection committee: Prime

XI.	Criminal trespass is defined under Section 329 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).
According to this provision, a person commits criminal trespass when they enter into or upon
property in the possession of another with the intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate,
insult, or annoy the person in possession of that property. Criminal trespass may also occur
when a person lawfully enters property but subsequently remains there unlawfully with the
intent to intimidate, insult, annoy the possessor, or commit an offence. In simple terms,
criminal trespass involves unauthorised entry into another person’s property or unlawful
remaining on the property with a wrongful intention. The essential ingredients of criminal
trespass include unlawful entry, possession of property by another person, unlawful remaining
even after lawful entry, and the presence of criminal intent. Examples include entering
someone’s private garden or farmland without permission, refusing to leave a place after being
asked to do so, or entering a fenced property without authorisation. The punishment for
criminal trespass under Section 329(3), BNS is imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine
up to %5,000, or both.
House trespass is a more serious form of criminal trespass and is defined under Section 330 of
the BNS. The concepts of house-trespass and house-breaking are dealt with in Section 330,
BNS. It occurs when criminal trespass is committed by entering or remaining in a building,
tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling, a place of worship, or a place for the custody of
property. House trespass therefore involves intrusion into private or protected spaces such as
homes, offices, religious institutions, or storage facilities. Even introducing any part of the
body, such as a hand through a window, may amount to house trespass. Examples include
breaking into someone’s house without permission, entering an office building with the
intention of committing theft, or unlawfully entering a temple, mosque, or church. The
punishment for house trespass under Section 329(4), BNS is imprisonment for up to one year,
or a fine up to 75,000, or both. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The key difference between criminal trespass and house trespass lies in the nature of the
property involved. Criminal trespass may occur on any property, including open land or fenced
areas, whereas house trespass specifically involves buildings or structures used for dwelling,
worship, or storage. Both offences require the same intent to commit an offence or to
intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor, but house trespass is treated as more serious
because it invades spaces associated with privacy and security. More aggravated forms also
exist, such as house-breaking, which is now covered under Section 330, BNS, and punishment
for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking is dealt with under Section 331, BNS. [Word
Count: 448]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://vakilsearch.com/bns/sections/329

XI.	Criminal trespass is defined under Section 329 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).
According to this provision, a person commits criminal trespass when they enter into or upon
property in the possession of another with the intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate,
insult, or annoy the person in possession of that property. Criminal trespass may also occur
when a person lawfully enters property but subsequently remains there unlawfully with the
intent to intimidate, insult, annoy the possessor, or commit an offence. In simple terms,
criminal trespass involves unauthorised entry into another person’s property or unlawful
remaining on the property with a wrongful intention. The essential ingredients of criminal
trespass include unlawful entry, possession of property by another person, unlawful remaining
even after lawful entry, and the presence of criminal intent. Examples include entering
someone’s private garden or farmland without permission, refusing to leave a place after being
asked to do so, or entering a fenced property without authorisation. The punishment for
criminal trespass under Section 329(3), BNS is imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine
up to %5,000, or both.
House trespass is a more serious form of criminal trespass and is defined under Section 330 of
the BNS. The concepts of house-trespass and house-breaking are dealt with in Section 330,
BNS. It occurs when criminal trespass is committed by entering or remaining in a building,
tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling, a place of worship, or a place for the custody of
property. House trespass therefore involves intrusion into private or protected spaces such as
homes, offices, religious institutions, or storage facilities. Even introducing any part of the
body, such as a hand through a window, may amount to house trespass. Examples include
breaking into someone’s house without permission, entering an office building with the
intention of committing theft, or unlawfully entering a temple, mosque, or church. The
punishment for house trespass under Section 329(4), BNS is imprisonment for up to one year,
or a fine up to 75,000, or both. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The key difference between criminal trespass and house trespass lies in the nature of the
property involved. Criminal trespass may occur on any property, including open land or fenced
areas, whereas house trespass specifically involves buildings or structures used for dwelling,
worship, or storage. Both offences require the same intent to commit an offence or to
intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor, but house trespass is treated as more serious
because it invades spaces associated with privacy and security. More aggravated forms also
exist, such as house-breaking, which is now covered under Section 330, BNS, and punishment
for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking is dealt with under Section 331, BNS. [Word
Count: 448]

XII. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 is a secular law enacted by Parliament to provide a civil form
of marriage for individuals irrespective of religion or faith. The concept of a secular marriage
law in India dates back to the nineteenth century during British rule, when marriage was
largely governed by religious customs. In 1872, Sir Henry Sumner Maine introduced Act III of
1872, known as the Special Marriage Act, 1872, to allow dissenters to marry under civil law.
However, the Act required parties to declare that they did not profess any religion, making it
impractical. After independence, the Special Marriage Act, 1954 replaced the earlier law and
allowed people of any religion to marry without renouncing their faith. The Act applies to all
Indian citizens, inter-religious and inter-caste couples, Indian nationals living abroad, and
marriages between an Indian citizen and a foreign national in India. It also connects with the
Foreign Marriage Act, 1969 for citizens domiciled abroad. Marriage under the Act is civil in
nature and is treated as a legal contract solemnised before a Marriage Officer and witnesses
rather than through religious rituals.

The conditions for a valid marriage are laid down in Section 4. Neither party should have a
living spouse, both parties must have the mental capacity to give valid consent, the male must
have completed 21 years and the female 18 years, and the parties must not fall within
prohibited degrees of relationship unless permitted by custom. The procedure for marriage
begins with a notice of intended marriage under Section 5, which must be given to the
Marriage Officer of the district where one party has resided for at least thirty days. The notice
is entered and published under Section 6, and objections can be raised within thirty days
under Sections 7—8 if the conditions of Section 4 are violated. Before solemnization, the parties
and three witnesses sign a declaration under Section 11, and the marriage is solemnized
under Section 12 by a verbal declaration before the Marriage Officer. After the ceremony, a
marriage certificate under Section 13 is issued, which is conclusive proof of marriage. If the
marriage is not solemnized within three months, the notice lapses under Section 14. Existing
marriages may also be registered under Sections 15-18.
The Act also regulates legal consequences and matrimonial remedies. Under Section 19, a
Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jaina marrying under this Act is deemed to sever from the joint
family, while succession is generally governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 under
Sections 20—21A. Children born from such marriages are legitimate. Matrimonial remedies
include restitution of conjugal rights (Section 22), judicial separation (Section 23), void and
voidable marriages (Sections 24-25), and divorce (Sections 27-28) on grounds such as
adultery, cruelty, desertion, imprisonment, mental disorder, venereal disease, or
disappearance for seven years. [Word Count: 471]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in

Allow registration, because people of any religion may marry without renouncing their

Refuse registration, because only same-faith couples can marry under this Act, and

Allow registration only after both parties convert to one religion, because conversion
supplies a common faith and removes legal objections for marriage.

content.passageText:
XIII. A quasi-contract is a legal remedy developed by courts to address situations where one party is
unjustly enriched at the expense of another, even though there is no formal agreement or
mutual consent between the parties. The term “quasi” comes from Latin meaning “as if,” and
therefore a quasi-contract is treated as if it were a contract despite lacking essential elements
such as offer, acceptance and consideration. Quasi-contractual obligations are imposed by law
to prevent unfair benefit and ensure that no individual gains at the expense of another. These
obligations are involuntary and arise without the intention of the parties, and their main
objective is restitution, which restores the aggrieved party to the position they were in before
the unjust enrichment occurred.
The key features of quasi-contracts include the absence of agreement between the parties, the
fact that they are imposed by law rather than created by consent, and the remedy of
restitution to compensate the party who suffered loss. The doctrine underlying quasi-contracts
is the doctrine of unjust enrichment, expressed in the maxim “Nemo debet locupletari ex
aliena jactura,” meaning no one should be enriched at another’s expense. In India, quasi-
contracts are codified under Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 68
deals with necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting, such as a minor, where
reimbursement can be claimed from the person’s property. Section 69 provides that a person
who pays money on behalf of another to protect their own interest is entitled to
reimbursement. Section 70 states that when a person lawfully provides goods or services
without intending them to be gratuitous and the other party benefits, the recipient must
compensate for the benefit. Section 71 imposes responsibility on a finder of goods to take
reasonable care and return them to the rightful owner. Section 72 provides that money paid by
mistake or under coercion must be returned.

The concept evolved from English common law and was articulated in the landmark case of
Moses v. MacFarlane (1760), where Lord Mansfield emphasised the obligation to refund
money received unjustly. Indian courts have also recognised this principle in cases such as
State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai (1964) and Hari Ram Sheth Khandsari v.
Commissioner of Sales Tax (1958), where restitution was ordered for money paid by mistake.
Unlike express contracts which are based on mutual consent and clearly defined terms, quasi-
contracts are imposed by law and apply only in limited situations to prevent unjust
enrichment. [Word Count: 413]

fail when no written contract exists at all.

XIV. Remedies for torts are broadly classified into judicial remedies and extra-judicial remedies.
Judicial remedies are those granted by courts of law to an aggrieved party, while extra-judicial
remedies are those where the injured party lawfully takes action without approaching the
court. The three principal judicial remedies are damages, injunction, and specific restitution of
property. Damages are the primary remedy in tort law and consist of monetary compensation
paid to restore the plaintiff, as far as money can, to the position they would have occupied had
the tort not occurred. Different types of damages are recognised: nominal damages where a
legal right is violated without actual loss, as in Ashby v. White and Constantine v. Imperial
London Hotels Ltd.; contemptuous damages where actual harm is trivial; compensatory
damages to restore actual loss; aggravated damages for additional injury such as humiliation,
pain, and loss of self-esteem; punitive or exemplary damages to punish the defendant and
deter similar conduct; and general and special damages, where general damages flow
naturally from the wrong while special damages must be specifically proved. However, only
damage that is not too remote is compensable, and courts apply principles of remoteness as
seen in Re Polemis and Liesbosch Dredger v. SS Edison.
Another important judicial remedy is injunction, which is an equitable remedy granted at the
discretion of the court. Instead of merely awarding money, the court restrains a person from
continuing a wrongful act or directs them to perform a positive act to undo the wrong.
Injunctions may be temporary or permanent, and mandatory or prohibitory, and are governed
by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Sections 37 to 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. In
M/s Hindustan Pencils Pvt. Ltd. v. India Stationery Products, injunction was granted to
restrain trademark infringement. The third judicial remedy is specific restitution of property,
which restores goods or property wrongfully taken from the owner.
Extra-judicial remedies allow a person to protect or recover their rights without court
intervention. These include expulsion of a trespasser, re-entry on land, re-caption of goods,
abatement of nuisance, and distress damage feasant, where a person may retain cattle or
beasts that have entered and damaged their property until compensation is made. These
remedies are lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances. [Word Count:
379]

torts /remedies-in-the-law-of-torts- 1106766

Which loss is least likely to be compensable?

All losses recoverable, because defendant takes victim as found, and remoteness never
limits damages in tort law today.

Only physical repair costs recoverable, because courts never compensate economic loss,
even if directly caused by negligence here.

All claimed profits recoverable, because once breach occurs, every subsequent financial
consequence is presumed foreseeable by law always.

Exclude the market-crash losses, because only damage that is not too remote is
compensable under tort principles here.

captures the cattle, ties them in a shed, and refuses to release them unless the neighbour pays

authorised by magistrate order first.

It is unlawful because courts alone may grant remedies, and private detention of cattle is
always a crime.

SECTION IV
XV. The Union Budget 2026-27 proposes to build a ‘strong care ecosystem’ by training 1.5 lakh
multiskilled caregivers in geriatric, core care and allied skills through programmes aligned
with the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF). As India’s care needs expand, such
a move is both timely and necessary. However, the Budget reveals a deeper paradox; even as
the state prepares to train a new cadre of certified care professionals, it makes little mention
of the five million plus women who already run India’s health, nutrition and childcare
systems. Our Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Anganwadi workers and helpers,
and mid-day meal workers continue to deliver essential public services every day, yet remain
classified as ‘volunteers’, excluded from the very ecosystem the state now seems determined to
strengthen. From the Anganwadi worker ensuring a child is fed to the ASHA worker tracking
a pregnancy in a remote village, these women constitute the backbone of India’s welfare
architecture. Their work is essential, continuous and indispensable to the state, yet they
labour in a deeply precarious space, earning meagre monthly honorariums, without formal
contracts, paid leaves or maternity benefits. What little support they receive comes from small
and fragmented responses by individual States such as honorarium hikes (which vary from
State to State) and gratuity benefits, or coverage under national schemes such as Ayushman
Bharat and Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan. But these piecemeal measures do little to
address the contradiction that lies at the core of India’s care economy — that the state relies
on a vast, feminised shadow labour force of women to deliver essential public services but
classifies them as ‘honorary workers’ to limit protections typically associated with formal
employment.
This contradiction is rooted in deeper structural norms surrounding care. The ‘care penalty’ in
India is not just a sociological concept, it is a statistical reality. Insights from the 2024 Time
Use Survey highlighted in the Economic Survey 2025-26 reinforce Indian women’s role as
primary caregivers, with 41% of females aged 15-59 spending 140 minutes daily on household
caregiving, compared to just 21.4% of males at 74 minutes. This pattern mirrors India’s
welfare architecture. By outsourcing its care responsibilities to women labelled as ‘volunteers’,
the state draws on long-standing social norms that view care work as an extension of a
woman’s domestic duty rather than skilled labour deserving fair compensation. Since care is
seen as ‘natural’ to women, it is rendered cheap and informal. This creates a vicious cycle —
the less care work is recognised as skilled, the less compulsion there is to pay for it, trapping a
predominantly female workforce in insecure employment.
[Word Count: 432]

ed/the-need-to-recognise-volunteer-care-work/article70719886.ece

The author views future-oriented care reform as inadequate when it avoids confronting the
status of those already sustaining public welfare delivery.

The author believes professional certification in care work will inevitably displace local
women currently embedded in welfare programmes.

The author treats State silence on existing workers as evidence that public care functions
should be shifted entirely outside government schemes.

content.passageText:
SECTION IV
XV. The Union Budget 2026-27 proposes to build a ‘strong care ecosystem’ by training 1.5 lakh
multiskilled caregivers in geriatric, core care and allied skills through programmes aligned
with the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF). As India’s care needs expand, such
a move is both timely and necessary. However, the Budget reveals a deeper paradox; even as
the state prepares to train a new cadre of certified care professionals, it makes little mention
of the five million plus women who already run India’s health, nutrition and childcare
systems. Our Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Anganwadi workers and helpers,
and mid-day meal workers continue to deliver essential public services every day, yet remain
classified as ‘volunteers’, excluded from the very ecosystem the state now seems determined to
strengthen. From the Anganwadi worker ensuring a child is fed to the ASHA worker tracking
a pregnancy in a remote village, these women constitute the backbone of India’s welfare
architecture. Their work is essential, continuous and indispensable to the state, yet they
labour in a deeply precarious space, earning meagre monthly honorariums, without formal
contracts, paid leaves or maternity benefits. What little support they receive comes from small
and fragmented responses by individual States such as honorarium hikes (which vary from
State to State) and gratuity benefits, or coverage under national schemes such as Ayushman
Bharat and Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan. But these piecemeal measures do little to
address the contradiction that lies at the core of India’s care economy — that the state relies
on a vast, feminised shadow labour force of women to deliver essential public services but
classifies them as ‘honorary workers’ to limit protections typically associated with formal
employment.
This contradiction is rooted in deeper structural norms surrounding care. The ‘care penalty’ in
India is not just a sociological concept, it is a statistical reality. Insights from the 2024 Time
Use Survey highlighted in the Economic Survey 2025-26 reinforce Indian women’s role as
primary caregivers, with 41% of females aged 15-59 spending 140 minutes daily on household
caregiving, compared to just 21.4% of males at 74 minutes. This pattern mirrors India’s
welfare architecture. By outsourcing its care responsibilities to women labelled as ‘volunteers’,
the state draws on long-standing social norms that view care work as an extension of a
woman’s domestic duty rather than skilled labour deserving fair compensation. Since care is
seen as ‘natural’ to women, it is rendered cheap and informal. This creates a vicious cycle —
the less care work is recognised as skilled, the less compulsion there is to pay for it, trapping a
predominantly female workforce in insecure employment.
[Word Count: 432]

ed/the-need-to-recognise-volunteer-care-work/article70719886.ece

preserves the “honorary” classification in order to limit the obligations linked to formal

New skilling programmes are being designed to increase the supply of caregivers in
geriatric, core care, and allied support services.

Public discourse in many regions continues to treat women’s caregiving labour as morally
admirable but economically secondary.

through nationally sponsored welfare schemes.

Official notes show that regularisation was proposed repeatedly but stalled due to fiscal
and constitutional disputes.

The passage suggests that the honorary classification is maintained so that the state can avoid the legal and financial responsibilities of formal employment.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the author’s criticism most strongly
depends?
options:
Work that requires sustained responsibility in delivering welfare outcomes should not be
dismissed as merely natural feminine disposition.

Labour central to welfare delivery should not be denied value merely because it resembles
duties traditionally performed within households.

Any expansion of skill-based certification necessarily creates a hierarchy between newly
trained workers and longstanding grassroots personnel.

The central state alone possesses both the authority and the obligation to redesign every
component of India’s care architecture.

The state expands formal care systems while still relying on workers whose labour

content.passageText:
XVI. Most of America “springs forward” Sunday for daylight saving time. Losing that hour of sleep
can do more than leave you tired and cranky the next day; it also could harm your health.
Darker mornings and more evening light knock your body clock out of whack — which means
daylight saving time can usher in sleep trouble for weeks or longer. Studies have even found
an uptick in heart attacks and strokes right after the March time change. There are ways to
ease the adjustment, including getting more sunshine to help reset your circadian rhythm for
healthful sleep.
Daylight saving time begins Sunday at 2 a.m., an hour of sleep vanishing in most of the U.S.
The ritual will reverse on Nov. 1 when clocks “fall back” as daylight saving time ends. Hawaii
and most of Arizona don’t make the spring switch, sticking to standard time year-round —
along with Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Worldwide,
dozens of countries also observe daylight saving time, starting and ending at different dates.
Some people try to prepare for daylight saving time by going to bed a little earlier two or three
nights ahead. While getting back on schedule after an hour’s change may not be that difficult
for some people, it’s an added challenge for the third of U.S. adults who already don’t get the
recommended seven hours of nightly shuteye. The brain has a master clock that is set by
exposure to sunlight and darkness. This circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour cycle that
determines when we become sleepy and when we're more alert. The patterns change with age,
one reason that early-to-rise youngsters evolve into hard-to-wake teens.
Morning light resets the rhythm. By evening, levels of a hormone called melatonin begin to
surge, triggering drowsiness. Too much light in the evening — that extra hour from daylight
saving time — delays that surge and the cycle gets out of sync. Sleep deprivation is linked to
heart disease, cognitive decline, obesity and numerous other problems. And that circadian
clock affects more than sleep, also influencing things like heart rate, blood pressure, stress
hormones and metabolism. Fatal car crashes temporarily jump the first few days after the
spring time change, according to a study of U.S. traffic fatalities. The risk was highest in the
morning, and researchers attributed it to sleep deprivation. Then there’s the cardiac
connection. The American Heart Association points to studies that suggest an uptick in heart
attacks on the Monday after daylight saving time begins, and in strokes for two days
afterward. Doctors already know that heart attacks, especially severe ones, are a bit more
common on Mondays generally — and in the morning, when blood is more clot-prone.
[Word Count: 451]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https: //indianexpress.com/article/lifestyle/health/how-daylight-saving-time-health-
10569374/

Which of the following, if true, most seriously challenges the author’s view that the spring
clock shift itself is a meaningful health hazard?
options:
Many urban workers describe the spring transition as irritating but still manageable
within a few days of routine adjustment.

Several countries continue the seasonal clock practice despite recurrent criticism from
physicians and sleep specialists.

The reported rise in post-shift medical events disappears after researchers control for
weekday stress and seasonal fluctuations.

Public dislike of darker winter mornings often outweighs concern about sleep disruption
among regular commuters.
content.explanation: directly undermines this by suggesting that when researchers account for confounding variables — weekday stress and seasonal fluctuations — the spike disappears entirely. This means the time change may be a coincidental correlation, not a cause.

content.questionText:
Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the author’s contention that the spring
transition produces harms beyond temporary inconvenience?
options:
Regions exempt from the spring clock advance show no comparable spike in sleep-related
emergencies during the same week.

Adults with flexible work hours generally report less resentment toward the spring change
than fixed-schedule employees.

Retail activity often rises after longer evenings begin because people spend more time
outside after work.

A majority of respondents say they notice the clock change mainly when discussing
schedules with friends and family.
content.explanation: provides a control group comparison: if regions that skip the spring change (Hawaii, Arizona, etc.) show no similar spike in sleep-related emergencies during the same week, it directly isolates the clock change as the causal variable. This rules out the alternative explanation that "it's just something about that time of year" and confirms the time change is the culprit — strongly supporting the author's argument.

content.questionText:
The reference to widespread pre-existing sleep shortage in adults primarily serves which
function in the author’s argument?
options:
It proves inadequate sleep-in adults is chiefly caused by official time policies rather than
social or behavioural habits.

It shows the clock shift operates on a population already susceptible to further disturbance
and reduced resilience.

It explains why the body clock changes naturally across the life span from childhood into
late adulthood.

It establishes that health authorities agree more strongly on sleep duration than on
cardiovascular risk patterns.
content.explanation: This option best captures the role of the statistic in the passage. The author is not saying that daylight saving time created the existing sleep shortage, but that the spring shift becomes more serious because many adults are already under slept.

Correctly timed morning light can assist the body in recovering from rhythm disruption

XVI. Most of America “springs forward” Sunday for daylight saving time. Losing that hour of sleep
can do more than leave you tired and cranky the next day; it also could harm your health.
Darker mornings and more evening light knock your body clock out of whack — which means
daylight saving time can usher in sleep trouble for weeks or longer. Studies have even found
an uptick in heart attacks and strokes right after the March time change. There are ways to
ease the adjustment, including getting more sunshine to help reset your circadian rhythm for
healthful sleep.
Daylight saving time begins Sunday at 2 a.m., an hour of sleep vanishing in most of the U.S.
The ritual will reverse on Nov. 1 when clocks “fall back” as daylight saving time ends. Hawaii
and most of Arizona don’t make the spring switch, sticking to standard time year-round —
along with Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Worldwide,
dozens of countries also observe daylight saving time, starting and ending at different dates.
Some people try to prepare for daylight saving time by going to bed a little earlier two or three
nights ahead. While getting back on schedule after an hour’s change may not be that difficult
for some people, it’s an added challenge for the third of U.S. adults who already don’t get the
recommended seven hours of nightly shuteye. The brain has a master clock that is set by
exposure to sunlight and darkness. This circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour cycle that
determines when we become sleepy and when we're more alert. The patterns change with age,
one reason that early-to-rise youngsters evolve into hard-to-wake teens.
Morning light resets the rhythm. By evening, levels of a hormone called melatonin begin to
surge, triggering drowsiness. Too much light in the evening — that extra hour from daylight
saving time — delays that surge and the cycle gets out of sync. Sleep deprivation is linked to
heart disease, cognitive decline, obesity and numerous other problems. And that circadian
clock affects more than sleep, also influencing things like heart rate, blood pressure, stress
hormones and metabolism. Fatal car crashes temporarily jump the first few days after the
spring time change, according to a study of U.S. traffic fatalities. The risk was highest in the
morning, and researchers attributed it to sleep deprivation. Then there’s the cardiac
connection. The American Heart Association points to studies that suggest an uptick in heart
attacks on the Monday after daylight saving time begins, and in strokes for two days
afterward. Doctors already know that heart attacks, especially severe ones, are a bit more
common on Mondays generally — and in the morning, when blood is more clot-prone.

XVII. Human identity is a captivating and intricate subject. One could argue that with the
emergence of digital platforms, and the widespread availability of more diverse media,
literature and learning opportunities than ever before, the way the average person defines
themselves has undergone a significant transformation. Unlike just a couple of decades ago,
when identity was often linked to one’s personal traits and role within one’s community, today
it is becoming increasingly entangled with the things we consume, especially online.
A compelling case study of this identity shift can be observed in TikTok culture. While trends
on this app emerge in a manner similar to trends spread through magazines and television in
the past (albeit at an incredibly accelerated pace), what’s striking on TikTok is how its users’
sense of themselves is increasingly intertwined with the clothes they wear, the media they
engage with, even the food they eat. Though the notion of products shaping identities was
famously propagated by Edward Bernays, the ‘father of public relations’, way back in the
1920s, this does underscore his profound understanding of human behavior.
Today it’s challenging to find individuals who primarily define themselves by their intrinsic
traits; instead, many tend to define themselves by what they consume. But alongside
straightforward promotion of the products themselves, there’s now a more subtle and insidious
marketing approach at play. These trends are strategically targeted towards women by
associating a particular combination of products with a particular type of woman. For

instance, a trend emerged wherein a mix of various new products, including specific clothing,
jewelry, and branded hair and makeup products, were promoted simultaneously. They were
marketed under the guise of the ‘clean girl’ trend. A ‘clean girl’ is essentially the kind of
woman who consistently appears well-groomed and put together, emanates a pleasant
fragrance, and boasts fresh, radiant skin. The marketing extends beyond the immediate
attributes of the products themselves: it represents an effort to emulate the image of the clean
girl, which is associated with a well-off, high-class lifestyle and a harmonious family
background. So this and other such approaches can be seen as a means for individuals to role-
play various personas they aspire to embody through the use of these products. This
transformation gives rise to a paradox: if individuals are so eager to distinguish themselves
from the crowd, why do they engage in these carefully orchestrated trends that essentially
commodify their identity, categorising them through consumerism? www.lawpreptutorial.com
The straightforward response is capitalism. Capitalism has wrought a profound shift in the
way we perceive ourselves and others. In a world driven by consumerism, competition and
envy, people are increasingly inclined to shape themselves into marketable entities by
endeavoring to make their identities palatable to a wide audience. [Word Count: 453]

in 15 days, and Suresh, the least experienced of the three, can finish it in 20 days.

previous assignment. From Day 3 onward, all three painters began working together and
continued jointly for 3 days. At the end of Day 5, Lakshmi had to leave for a family function.
Manoj and Suresh carried on and completed whatever work remained. The Gram Sabha
decided to pay a total of 745,000, distributed among the three painters in proportion to the
work each one had done.
Separately, a smaller meeting hall requiring exactly half the work of the main hall also needed
painting. Lakshmi and Manoj took up this job and estimated they could finish in 5 days
working 8 hours per day. However, due to daily power outages, they could work only 5 hours
each day and wanted to recalculate their schedule.

content.explanation: First 2 days (Lakshmi alone) = 1/6. Days 3-5 (all three together): Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 5/60 + 4/60 + 3/60 = 12/60 = 1/5 per day.

XX. In the town of Rampur, the community hall needed a fresh coat of paint before the annual fair.

working 8 hours per day. However, due to daily power outages, they could work only 5 hours
each day and wanted to recalculate their schedule.

SECTION I
I	In a stretch of desert north of Cairo, a small fragment of jawbone is forcing a rethink of where
the story of modern apes, including humans, may have begun. The fossil belongs to a newly
identified species, Masripithecus moghraensis, which lived about 17 to 18 million years ago
during the Early Miocene. Described in Science, the fossil was found at Wadi Moghra and is
the first definitive ape from North Africa from this time period — pointing to Egypt, and
possibly the wider North Africa—Middle East region, as a key region in the origin of living
apes, helping fill a gap in the early history of crown Hominoidea, the group that includes all
living apes and their last common ancestor. We spent five years searching for this kind of
fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that
something is missing — and North Africa holds that missing piece.
Until now, Early Miocene sites in North Africa had turned up monkeys, but not apes. That gap
helped shape the view that early apes and their close relatives were restricted to more
southern parts of Africa during this period. Younger ape fossils have been found across Africa,
Asia, and Europe, but their relationships and the group's first emergence remain debated.
Masripithecus shows that apes lived in North Africa during the Early Miocene and that the
species was distinct from similarly aged East African apes, suggesting the fossil record has
been missing part of the record of where the earliest branches of the ape family diversified.
Masripithecus combines Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt, with the Greek word for ape. The
species name, moghraensis, refers to Wadi Moghra, where the remains were recovered in 2023
and 2024.
The fossil consists of a lower jaw, but it preserves a combination of features not seen in any
other known ape from this time. The jaw is robust, with large canine and premolar teeth and
rounded, textured molars. This suggests Masripithecus had a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet,
with the ability to process tougher foods, such as nuts and seeds, when needed. That flexibility
would have been useful in a region becoming more seasonal, where climatic shifts in northern
Africa and Arabia made food supplies less predictable. [Word Count: 377]

described in the passage?

It weakens older geographic assumptions about early ape emergence.
It shows that North African monkeys directly developed into apes.
It settles every major dispute about the crown Hominoidea lineage.

I	In a stretch of desert north of Cairo, a small fragment of jawbone is forcing a rethink of where
the story of modern apes, including humans, may have begun. The fossil belongs to a newly
identified species, Masripithecus moghraensis, which lived about 17 to 18 million years ago
during the Early Miocene. Described in Science, the fossil was found at Wadi Moghra and is
the first definitive ape from North Africa from this time period — pointing to Egypt, and
possibly the wider North Africa—Middle East region, as a key region in the origin of living
apes, helping fill a gap in the early history of crown Hominoidea, the group that includes all
living apes and their last common ancestor. We spent five years searching for this kind of
fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that
something is missing — and North Africa holds that missing piece.
Until now, Early Miocene sites in North Africa had turned up monkeys, but not apes. That gap
helped shape the view that early apes and their close relatives were restricted to more
southern parts of Africa during this period. Younger ape fossils have been found across Africa,
Asia, and Europe, but their relationships and the group's first emergence remain debated.
Masripithecus shows that apes lived in North Africa during the Early Miocene and that the
species was distinct from similarly aged East African apes, suggesting the fossil record has
been missing part of the record of where the earliest branches of the ape family diversified.
Masripithecus combines Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt, with the Greek word for ape. The
species name, moghraensis, refers to Wadi Moghra, where the remains were recovered in 2023
and 2024.
The fossil consists of a lower jaw, but it preserves a combination of features not seen in any
other known ape from this time. The jaw is robust, with large canine and premolar teeth and
rounded, textured molars. This suggests Masripithecus had a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet,
with the ability to process tougher foods, such as nuts and seeds, when needed. That flexibility
would have been useful in a region becoming more seasonal, where climatic shifts in northern
Africa and Arabia made food supplies less predictable. [Word Count: 377]

I.	Administrative data has emerged as a powerful and strategic asset for modern governance and
decision-making. Generated as a byproduct of routine administrative processes, it offers
granular insights not only for decision-making but also to enable governments and institutions
to move towards more continuous and comprehensive data systems.
In India, over the past decade, the growing digitalisation of public services has led to a
substantial increase in the availability of digital data across diverse socio-economic
dimensions. Almost every ministry and department at the Centre and in states/UTs now relies
on internal MIS systems and dashboards that collect and collate data from stakeholders.

Examples include the Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE) for school
education, Udyam for MSMEs, Prime Minister’s Overarching Scheme for Holistic
Nourishment (POSHAN) Tracker for child nutrition, Aadhaar, GSTN data and Health MIS.
While these systems provide significant value within individual departments, their impact can
be enhanced through harmonisation of datasets, enabling information from different sources
to be combined to generate more meaningful insights. The vast volume and diversity of
administrative datasets make them highly suitable for advanced analytics using AI and
machine learning. As datasets become increasingly discoverable, machine-readable,
consistent, and easier to integrate, their analytical potential expands. In this context, the
growing focus on “Al-ready” data highlights the importance of data harmonisation.
By strengthening standardisation, ensuring uniformity in concepts and definitions, and
enabling interoperability, data harmonisation makes it possible to transform isolated datasets
into a coherent whole. To support these outcomes, a structured and enabling environment is
being established, anchored in five pillars: Clear documentation of what the data represents,
how it is collected, and how it can be used (metadata); ensuring accuracy and reliability (data
quality); adopting common definitions and classification frameworks (standards and
classifications); establishing unique identifiers to enable linkage across datasets and carefully
reconciling differences. [Word Count: 302]
Sources: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/how-to-make-data-tell-a-larger-story-
drive-smarter-policy-10617948/

Which statement is best supported by the passage as evidence of administrative data’s
strategic value?

It matters chiefly because ministries already possess it.
It can connect routine records to deeper public insight.
content.explanation: This option most accurately reflects the reasoning of the passage. Administrative data is valuable not simply because it exists, but because routine records can yield granular insights that support better decision-making and more continuous public data systems.

Il.	In the library, I watch people navigate information in ways that would have seemed
impossible to previous generations. A research question that once required weeks of archival
work now takes hours. But more than efficiency has changed. The nature of synthesis itself
has transformed. Ideas now move through multiple channels simultaneously. A documentary
provides emotional resonance and visual evidence. Its transcript enables the precision needed
to locate a specific argument. A newsletter unpacks the implications. A podcast allows the
ideas to marinate during a commute. Each mode contributes something the others cannot.
This isn’t decline. It's an expansion.
What strikes me most is the difference between people who've learned to construct what I call
‘containers for attention’ — bounded spaces and practices where different modes of engagement
become possible — and those who haven't. The distinction isn’t about intelligence or discipline.
It’s about environmental architecture. Some people have learned to watch documentaries with
a notebook, listen to podcasts during walks when their minds can wander productively, and
read physical books in deliberately quiet spaces with phones left behind. They're not rejecting
technology. They’re choreographing it.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Others are drowning, attempting sustained thought in environments engineered to prevent it.
They sit with laptops open, seven tabs competing for attention, notifications sliding in from
three different apps, phones vibrating every few minutes. They're trying to read serious
material while fighting a losing battle against behavioural psychology weaponised at scale.

They believe their inability to focus is a personal failure rather than a design problem. They
don’t realise they’re trying to think in a space optimised to prevent thinking. This is where my
understanding of literacy has fundamentally shifted. I used to believe, as I was taught, that
literacy was primarily about decoding text. But watching how people actually learn and think
has convinced me that literacy is about something deeper: the capacity to construct and
navigate environments where understanding becomes possible. [Word Count: 316]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://aeon.co/essays /what-we-think-is-a-
decline-in-literacy-is-a-design-problem

Concentration fails mainly because modern material is too dense.
content.explanation: This option most accurately captures the author’s larger argument because it converts the phrase “environmental architecture” into its underlying idea: thought depends heavily on designed conditions. The passage repeatedly contrasts intentionally structured settings with chaotic ones that undermine attention.

IV.	People should have an emergency stockpile of food in their homes in case conflicts, extreme
weather or cyber-attacks shut down supplies, leading UK experts have said. In an ever more
turbulent world, they say it is essential to choose long-life items that can be eaten without
cooking — think tinned beans, vegetables and fish, rice crackers, and oats that can be soaked.
But it is also important to choose items you actually like to eat, and some treats such as
chocolate or crisps to keep your spirits up. You will also need water — lots of it — not just to
drink but for washing too. Perhaps the most surprising advice is to be prepared to share your
stockpile with neighbours. With one in seven households with children already suffering food
insecurity in the UK, many people cannot afford to build up a stockpile and, without food, civil
unrest soon follows.
Yes, do store food, but be prepared to share to maintain social solidarity. All resilience theory
and experience, in shocks, wars, or sub-war conflicts, shows it is essential to maintain social
cohesion if you want to maintain social order. One shock could spark social unrest and even
food riots in the UK, according to a report from dozens of the country’s top food experts. They
said chronic issues like low incomes and fragile “just-in-time” supply chains have left the food
system a “tinderbox”. The Iran war, hitting vital fuel and fertiliser supplies to farmers, has
added to the pressure. in early March that the British government should be stockpiling food —
unlike Switzerland and many others, it is not. A recently uncovered government report from
2024 also warned that hits to the nation’s food security from the climate crisis and geopolitical
instability meant it could be “at strategic risk of catastrophic failure” by 2030. A spokesperson
for the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the country had a high
degree of food security, built on both strong domestic production and imports through stable
trade routes. The UK produces about 60% of its food domestically, while the US, France and
Australia are all food self-sufficient, and the Netherlands is 80% self-sufficient. [Word Count:
360]

VI.	International Women’s Day (IWD) is an annual global celebration that aims to educate society
on the remarkable women’s rights movement. This day marks a call to action for accelerating
gender parity, highlighting the ongoing efforts for continued advocacy and action worldwide,
and celebrating the cultural, political, and socio-economic achievements of women and girls.
It provides a global platform for collective action and collaboration in campaigning for women’s
rights and empowerment, breaking down barriers for women and girls all around the world.
The theme for International Women's Day intends to promote generosity and collaboration,
highlighting how reciprocal support creates more opportunities for women, as mentioned on
the IWD official website. Several demonstrations in demand of women’s franchise and political
rights of “proletarian” women or women workers have preceded Women's Day.
In the early twentieth century, the garments industry was the single largest employer of
women. However, the working women had to grapple with poor working conditions, long work
hours, and paltry wages. Most of these garment workers were engaged in an internal
subcontracting system that made extensive use of homework and marked their positions in the
production cycle as learners but not “skilled” labourers, thus they received meagre wages
compared to semi-skilled male operators. Their work hours were as long as 75 hours a week
and they were in some cases even required to supply their basic materials such as needles and
threads. They were fined for being late at work, and during their working hours, they were
locked up inside the workshop to stop them from taking breaks.

VIII. Chief Election Commissioner Rajiv Kumar asked all political parties and their leaders to
strictly adhere to the MCC, which lays down a list of dos and don’ts for leaders and parties
ahead of elections. Amongst other things, the code bars the government from announcing
policy decisions. The MCC comes into force from the date the election schedule is announced
until the date that results are out. As soon as the code kicks in, the party in power — whether
at the Centre or in the states — should ensure that it does not use its official position for
campaigning. Hence, no policy, project or scheme can be announced that can influence the
voting behaviour. The party must also avoid advertising at the cost of the public exchequer or
using official mass media for publicity on achievements to improve chances of victory in the
elections.
The code also says the ministers must not combine official visits with election work or use
official machinery for the same. The ruling party cannot use government transport or
machinery for campaigning. It should also ensure that public places such as maidans etc., for
holding election meetings, and facilities like the use of helipads are provided to the opposition
parties on the same terms and conditions on which they are used by the party in power. The
issue of advertisement at the cost of public exchequer in the newspapers and other media is
also considered an offence. The ruling government cannot make any ad-hoc appointments in
government, public sector undertakings etc., which may influence the voters.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https://indianexpress.com/article /explained /model-code-of-conduct-meaning-9217688/

IX.	Is the digital landscape quietly making a generation less happy? The answer, according to the
latest World Happiness Report 2026, appears to be yes. Heavy social media use seems to be
contributing to a drop in wellbeing among young people in English-speaking countries and
Western Europe, especially among girls, according to the report’s findings.
Data from Latin America show that the type of platform is crucial. Those designed to facilitate
social connections show a clear positive association with happiness, whereas those driven by
algorithmically curated content tend to demonstrate a negative association at high rates of
use. The report also found that nations in or near zones of major conflict remain at the foot of
the rankings. These rankings, according to the report, are based on a three-year average of
each population’s average assessment of their quality of life. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The global evidence makes clear that the links between social media use and our wellbeing
heavily depends on what platforms we’re using, who’s using them and how, as well as for how
long. Heavy usage is associated with much lower wellbeing, but those deliberately off social
media also appear to be missing out on some positive effects. Beyond the complexity, it is clear
that we should look as much as possible to put the ‘social’ back into social media.
The findings describe a complex global picture at a time when many countries are seeking to
implement greater legislative protections for those aged under 16 online.

XI.	The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 was enacted to ensure that Muslims
in India are governed by Islamic law in personal matters instead of inconsistent regional or
tribal customs. Before 1937, courts often relied on local usage rather than Quranic principles,
which created uncertainty and diluted uniform application of Muslim personal law. In
response to demands from Muslim scholars and leaders, the British Indian legislature passed
this Act, making Shariat the rule of decision in specified matters. The Act was therefore a
major reform measure, as it gave legal recognition to Islamic personal law within the Indian
legal framework and aimed to preserve the religious and cultural identity of Muslims while
replacing contrary customs.
The Act is short but legally important. Section 1 gives its title and extends it to the whole of
India, later fully extended through subsequent amendments. Section 2 is the heart of the Act.
It begins with the overriding phrase “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary”
and provides that in matters such as intestate succession, special property of females,
marriage, dissolution of marriage including talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula and mubaraat,
maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts, trust properties and wakfs, the rule of
decision for Muslims shall be Muslim Personal Law (Shariat). However, agricultural land is
excluded, which has often been criticised because this exclusion affected inheritance rights,
particularly of Muslim women, in agricultural property.
Section 3 gives a Muslim person the option to make a declaration for extending the application
of Shariat to additional matters not automatically covered under Section 2, such as adoption,
wills and legacies, provided the person is Muslim, competent to contract under Section 11 of
the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and resident within the territories to which the Act applies.
Such declaration, once accepted, binds not only the declarant but also minor children and
descendants. Section 4 empowers the State Government to frame procedural rules regarding
declarations, prescribed authorities, form, and fees, and these rules must be published and
laid before the State Legislature. Section 5 was later repealed by the Dissolution of Muslim
Marriages Act, 1939, and Section 6 repeals earlier inconsistent regional laws to secure
uniformity.
Judicial interpretation has further shaped the Act’s significance. In Shah Bano Begum v.
Mohd. Ahmed Khan (1985), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman could

claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, highlighting the interaction between personal
law and secular law. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Court declared triple talaq
unconstitutional, holding that it was not protected as an essential religious practice. In
Sameena Begum v. Union of India (2018), issues such as polygamy and nikah halala were
questioned, reflecting the continuing constitutional debate on reform, equality, and gender
justice within Muslim personal law. [Word Count: 460]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/the-muslim-
personal-law-shariat-act-1937/

in India are governed by Islamic law in personal matters instead of inconsistent regional or
tribal customs. Before 1937, courts often relied on local usage rather than Quranic principles,
which created uncertainty and diluted uniform application of Muslim personal law. In
response to demands from Muslim scholars and leaders, the British Indian legislature passed
this Act, making Shariat the rule of decision in specified matters. The Act was therefore a
major reform measure, as it gave legal recognition to Islamic personal law within the Indian
legal framework and aimed to preserve the religious and cultural identity of Muslims while
replacing contrary customs.
The Act is short but legally important. Section 1 gives its title and extends it to the whole of
India, later fully extended through subsequent amendments. Section 2 is the heart of the Act.
It begins with the overriding phrase “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary”
and provides that in matters such as intestate succession, special property of females,
marriage, dissolution of marriage including talaq, ila, zihar, lian, khula and mubaraat,
maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts, trust properties and wakfs, the rule of
decision for Muslims shall be Muslim Personal Law (Shariat). However, agricultural land is
excluded, which has often been criticised because this exclusion affected inheritance rights,
particularly of Muslim women, in agricultural property.
Section 3 gives a Muslim person the option to make a declaration for extending the application
of Shariat to additional matters not automatically covered under Section 2, such as adoption,
wills and legacies, provided the person is Muslim, competent to contract under Section 11 of
the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and resident within the territories to which the Act applies.
Such declaration, once accepted, binds not only the declarant but also minor children and
descendants. Section 4 empowers the State Government to frame procedural rules regarding
declarations, prescribed authorities, form, and fees, and these rules must be published and
laid before the State Legislature. Section 5 was later repealed by the Dissolution of Muslim
Marriages Act, 1939, and Section 6 repeals earlier inconsistent regional laws to secure
uniformity.
Judicial interpretation has further shaped the Act’s significance. In Shah Bano Begum v.
Mohd. Ahmed Khan (1985), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman could

claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, highlighting the interaction between personal
law and secular law. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Court declared triple talaq
unconstitutional, holding that it was not protected as an essential religious practice. In
Sameena Begum v. Union of India (2018), issues such as polygamy and nikah halala were
questioned, reflecting the continuing constitutional debate on reform, equality, and gender
justice within Muslim personal law. [Word Count: 460]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/the-muslim-
personal-law-shariat-act-1937/
content.questionText:
A Muslim businessman wants his adopted daughter to inherit as per Islamic principles rather
than local customary practice. He files a formal declaration before the prescribed authority to
extend Shariat to adoption and wills, asserting he is Muslim, adult, and resident in the area
where the Act applies. His cousin challenges the declaration, saying the statute cannot be
voluntarily extended and applies only to matters already listed under Section 2. The
businessman argues the Act itself provides an option to make such a declaration for additional
matters.
Which position best fits?
options:
Declaration invalid because Shariat can never be extended by choice; only Parliament may
add matters and individuals cannot opt-in.

Declaration valid because Section 3 gives a Muslim person the option to make a
declaration extending Shariat to adoption, wills and legacies.

Declaration invalid because adoption and wills are already covered in Section 2, so no
declaration is necessary and authority lacks power.

Declaration valid only if cousin consents, because family rights are collective and personal
declarations cannot bind relatives at all.

content.questionText:
A Muslim woman makes a valid declaration under the Act extending Shariat to wills and
legacies. Years later, her minor son becomes involved in a dispute about a legacy left by his
grandfather. Relatives argue the declaration binds only the woman personally and cannot
affect minors or descendants, so customary rules should still apply to the child’s legacy
dispute. The woman argues that once the declaration is accepted, its effect extends to her
minor children and descendants as well.
Which statement best matches the passage?
options:
Declaration binds only declarant, so minors and descendants are free to choose custom and
cannot be bound by parent’s declaration.

Declaration binds only the declarant’s spouse, because only marital unit is covered;
children and descendants are excluded always.

Declaration binds declarant plus minor children and descendants, so accepted declaration
extends its effect beyond the individual alone.

Declaration binds only after minors attain majority, because legal effect is suspended until
children can consent at age eighteen.

content.questionText:
A State government issues rules prescribing the authority, form, and fee for making
declarations under Section 3. A citizen challenges the rules, arguing the government has no
power to regulate declarations and that such matters must be left to courts. The State replies
it can frame procedural rules regarding declarations and must publish them and lay them
before the State Legislature for oversight.
Which statement best matches the Act’s description?
options:
State cannot frame rules because declarations are religious matters, and governments
cannot regulate them through any notified rules today.

State can frame procedural rules regarding declarations, prescribed authorities, form, and
fees, and such rules must be published and laid.

State can frame rules only if Parliament approves each declaration; otherwise rules are
invalid and cannot control any declaration filing.

State can frame rules, but it need not publish or lay them, because declaration rules are
purely internal administrative circulars.

A dispute arises where an old regional regulation allows a custom-based divorce practice
differing from Shariat principles. A party argues the regional law still applies because it
predates 1937 and has not been expressly repealed in local statutes. The other party argues
the Act was designed to secure uniformity and therefore repeals earlier inconsistent regional
laws, making Shariat the rule of decision in listed matters.
Which statement best reflects the Act’s effect on inconsistent older laws?
options:
Earlier inconsistent regional laws are repealed to secure uniformity, so local regulations
contrary to the Act cannot continue in force.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive because they are older, and later Acts cannot
override local traditions without explicit state consent always.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive unless courts declare them unconstitutional,
because statutory repeal requires constitutional litigation, not ordinary application.

Earlier inconsistent regional laws survive for marriage only, because uniformity applies
only to inheritance and trusts, not to divorce matters here.

content.questionText:
A Muslim man in a village dies intestate, leaving a widow and two daughters. The local
panchayat applies an old regional custom under which daughters do not inherit ancestral
house property, and the deceased’s brother is awarded the entire house. The widow
approaches a civil court, arguing that the personal law statute overrides “custom or usage to
the contrary” ” and makes Shariat the rule of decision for intestate succession. The brother
argues the custom is ancient and must prevail locally.
Which view best fits the Act’s rule?
options:
Custom prevails because village usage is the strongest source, and statutory personal law
cannot override it in family property matters.

Shariat prevails because Section 2 begins with “notwithstanding any custom or usage to
the contrary” for intestate succession.

Custom prevails because only marriage and talaq are covered; intestate succession is
excluded and left to local practices today.

Shariat prevails only if parties signed a declaration, because Section 2 applies only when a
Section 3 declaration is filed first.
content.explanation: This option directly uses “notwithstanding any custom or usage to the contrary” and ties it to “intestate succession,” matching the reference line’s words. Therefore, the court should treat Shariat as the rule of decision and not apply the panchayat custom that excludes daughters.

XII. Treaties are one of the principal sources of international law and are recognised under Article
88(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice along with custom, general principles,
and judicial decisions and teachings of highly qualified publicists. They are formal written
agreements by which States bind themselves in matters of international responsibility,
cooperation, organisation, trade, security, and rights. The modern law governing treaties is
primarily contained in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, which came into
force on 27 January 1980. Article 2(1)(a) of the Convention defines a treaty as an international
agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law,
whether contained in one or more related instruments and whatever its designation. The
binding basis of treaty law is the principle of pacta sunt servanda, recognised in Article 26,
which requires every treaty in force to be performed in good faith. Although, as a rule, only
signatory or ratifying States are bound, the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases recognised
that some treaties may have a norm-creating character. States may also enter reservations
under Article 2(1)(d), but reservations cannot defeat the object and purpose of the treaty.
Treaties may broadly be classified as law-making treaties and contractual treaties. Law-
making treaties are generally multilateral and create general binding norms, often in fields
such as human rights, maritime law, international mandates, tribunals, and waterways. They
resemble legislation and impose duties independent of private bargains. Contractual treaties,
on the other hand, are usually bilateral or limited in scope, and are based on mutual benefit,
such as trade, alliance, or conveyance agreements. The Vienna Convention governs the
making of treaties through stages such as adoption, authentication, expression of consent,
ratification, accession, and reservations. Ratification reflects approval, while accession refers
to becoming a party after the minimum ratification requirement has been met. Under Articles
34 to 37, third States are generally neither bound nor benefited by a treaty without their
consent, though customary international law may eventually make some treaty rules binding
more broadly.
The Convention also regulates invalidity, suspension, and termination. Under Articles 46 to
58, a treaty may be invalidated for conflict with domestic law regarding competence, error,
fraud, corruption, coercion, or conflict with jus cogens, that is, peremptory norms such as
genocide, piracy, apartheid, or torture. A treaty may terminate by withdrawal, breach,
impossibility of performance, conclusion of a later treaty on the same subject, fundamental
change of circumstances, or emergence of a new jus cogens norm. Thus, treaties remain a
central instrument of international law because they create legal certainty, regulate inter-
State conduct, and promote peace, order, and cooperation in the international system. [Word
Count: 434]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/law-of-treaties-in-
international-law/

States A and B sign a document titled “Green Shipping Protocol,” setting binding emission
caps for their state-owned shipping fleets. The protocol is in writing, signed by authorised
representatives, and states disputes will be resolved under international law. Later, State A
argues the instrument is not a treaty because it is called a “protocol,” not a “treaty,” and
therefore it is not legally binding. State B sues before an international tribunal claiming it is a
treaty regardless of name.
Which position best follows?
options:
Not a treaty because only documents named “treaty” count; protocols and memoranda are
political and non-binding always.

It is a treaty because an international agreement in written form governed by
international law is a treaty whatever its designation.

Not a treaty because treaties must be one single instrument only; a protocol is not a treaty
if it has annexures.

It is a treaty only if registered at the UN; without registration it remains unenforceable
and purely voluntary between States.

XIII. A trademark is a mark, symbol, word, phrase, design, shape, packaging, or colour combination
that distinguishes the goods or services of one person from those of others. Under Section
2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, it must be capable of graphical representation and
capable of distinguishing goods or services. The Act was enacted to protect business goodwill,
prevent consumer deception, promote fair competition, harmonise Indian law with
international instruments such as TRIPS and the Paris Convention, and simplify registration
and enforcement. Its important features include recognition of service marks, collective marks,
multi-class applications, protection of well-known marks, and registration valid for ten years,
renewable indefinitely. The Act follows the Nice Classification, dividing trademarks into 45
classes, with Classes 1-34 for goods and Classes 35—45 for services.
Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trademark may apply for registration by
submitting the applicant’s details, a clear representation of the mark, the relevant goods or
services with class numbers, date of first use if any, and priority details where applicable. The
Registrar examines the application on formal requirements, absolute grounds under Section 9,
and relative grounds under Section 11. Absolute refusal applies where the mark lacks
distinctiveness, is descriptive, deceptive, scandalous, functional, or uses protected emblems.
Relative refusal applies where the mark is identical or deceptively similar to an earlier mark,
causes confusion, infringes a well-known mark, or is otherwise prohibited by law. If accepted,
the mark is published in the Trade Marks Journal, after which any person may file opposition
within three months, extendable by one month. Opposition is followed by counter-statement,
evidence, hearing, and decision. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Registration gives the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark, stop others from using
confusingly similar marks, assign or license it, seek customs protection, and rely on it as
prima facie evidence of ownership. Section 29 defines infringement as unauthorised use of an
identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services in the
course of trade. Remedies include injunctions, damages, account of profits, delivery up,
destruction, Anton Piller orders, and restraining orders. Section 103 also prescribes criminal
penalties for false trademark use. Even unregistered marks are protected through passing off
under Section 27, if the plaintiff proves goodwill, misrepresentation, and likely damage. The
Act also recognises acquired distinctiveness, and regulates assignment, licensing, rectification,
restoration, and removal for non-use. After abolition of the IPAB in 2021, appeals and
rectification matters now lie directly before the High Courts. [Word Count: 413]

XIV. The ongoing Sabarimala reference before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court has revived
a foundational constitutional debate on the relationship between Articles 25 and 26 and the
continued validity of the Essential Religious Practice (ERP) test. The ERP test emerged from
an obiter observation in Durgah Committee v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961), where the Court
stated that only those practices which are “essential and integral” to a religion deserve
protection under Article 26. This modified the earlier approach in Shirur Mutt (1954), where
the Court had principally distinguished between secular practices, which can be regulated,
and religious practices, which receive constitutional protection. The present reference
therefore raises a central issue: whether courts should continue identifying essential religious
practices, or whether the inquiry should only be whether a practice is religious or secular.
During the hearing, Justice BV Nagarathna suggested that once a practice is determined to be
strictly secular, everything else would fall within the religious sphere, making the ERP test
unnecessary. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, however, noted that even such a distinction
would still require the Court to evolve standards for deciding what counts as religious and
what counts as secular, thereby bringing the inquiry back to the same constitutional problem.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan argued that the ERP test should be abandoned
because Articles 25 and 26 themselves are clear, and that religious affairs should be
understood through the constitutional text rather than broad judicial labels. In his
submission, Article 25(1), which is expressly made “subject to the other provisions” of Part III,
should be read as subject mainly to horizontal equality provisions such as Articles 15(2), 17,
23, and 24, whereas Article 26 stands on a stronger footing because it does not contain the
same phrase.
A major interpretive issue is whether Article 26(b), which protects a denomination’s right to
manage its own affairs in matters of religion, is subject to Article 25(2)(b), which permits the
State to enact laws for social reform and temple entry for all classes and sections of Hindus.
Article 25(2)(b) permits the State to make laws for social welfare and reform, including
throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of
Hindus. Article 26(b) protects a denomination’s right to manage its own affairs in matters of
religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Sai Deepak argued that Article 26 is not
controlled by Article 25(2), and that denominational rights were deliberately insulated from
broader constitutional limitations. In contrast, Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium argued
that Article 26 must be harmonised with Article 25(2)(a) and (b), so that denominational
temples may still be subject to reform laws opening access to excluded classes. Thus, the
reference now squarely presents two major constitutional questions: whether the ERP doctrine
should survive, and how individual religious freedom under Article 25 must be reconciled with
collective denominational autonomy under Article 26. [Word Count: 484]
